citations.quote: Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].
For a $C^2$ scalar field $f$, $H_f(a)^T=H_f(a)$ at every point $a$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and let $q_0\in\Omega$ be a local minimum of $U$: there is $\rho>0$ with $\overline B(q_0,\rho)\subseteq\Omega$ and $U(q)\ge U(q_0)$ for every $q\in\overline B(q_0,\rho)$. Then

$$\nabla U(q_0)=0,\qquad h^{\mathsf T}D^2U(q_0)h\ge0\quad\text{for every }h\in\mathbb R^n,$$

where $D^2U(q_0)$ is the Hessian matrix, which is symmetric ([[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]], [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite matrices, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, and let $q_0\in\Omega$ be a mechanical equilibrium, that is $\nabla U(q_0)=0$ ([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]). Let $G$ be the mechanical vector field on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$. Then:

1. $G$ is totally differentiable at $(q_0,0)$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]) and, writing $D^2U(q_0)$ for the Hessian matrix ([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]),

$$DG(q_0,0)(\delta q,\delta v)=\Bigl(\delta v,\ -M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)\,\delta q\Bigr)\qquad(\delta q,\delta v\in\mathbb R^n);$$

2. consequently the linearised equation at the equilibrium is

$$\xi''=-M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)\,\xi,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad M(q_0)\xi''+D^2U(q_0)\,\xi=0,$$

a constant-coefficient system whose mass matrix $M(q_0)$ is symmetric positive definite and whose stiffness matrix $D^2U(q_0)$ is symmetric ([[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]]);
3. if in addition $q_0$ is a strict local minimum of $U$, then $K:=D^2U(q_0)$ is non-negative, so the hypotheses of [[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]] are satisfied by $M(q_0)$ and $K$, and the linearised system is exactly the constant-coefficient quadratic system of that theorem with mass matrix $M(q_0)$ and stiffness $K$; its modes are the normal modes of the linearisation.

Let $n\ge1$, let $M\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric positive definite and let $K\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric and non-negative, that is $v^{\mathsf T}Kv\ge0$ for all $v\in\mathbb R^n$. Let $M^{1/2}$, $M^{-1/2}$ be the square roots of [[lem-cm-positive-definite-matrix-square-roots]] and let

$$S:=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}.$$

By the real spectral theorem choose an orthogonal matrix $O$ and a diagonal matrix $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$ with $S=O\Lambda O^{\mathsf T}$ and $\lambda_i\ge0$ for all $i$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ contain at least two points and satisfy $r,s\in I,\ r\le u\le s\Longrightarrow u\in I$ for all $r,s,u\in\mathbb R$; suppose also $0\in I$. Let $q:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be twice differentiable with continuous first and second domain-relative derivatives, in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]. Put $z:=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$. Then:

1. $q$ satisfies the quadratic system $Mq''+Kq=0$ on $I$ if and only if $z$ satisfies the decoupled system

$$z_i''+\lambda_iz_i=0\qquad(1\le i\le n)$$

on $I$;
2. for every $i$ the solutions of the scalar equation in clause 1 on an interval containing $0$, with prescribed initial data, are exactly as follows:

$$z_i(t)=a_i\cos(\omega_it)+b_i\sin(\omega_it)\quad\text{with }\omega_i:=\sqrt{\lambda_i}>0\ \text{when }\lambda_i>0,$$

equivalently $z_i(t)=\operatorname{Re}(C_ie^{i\omega_it})$ with $C_i=a_i-ib_i\in\mathbb C$, and

$$z_i(t)=a_i+b_it\qquad\text{when }\lambda_i=0;$$

the coefficients are $a_i=z_i(0)$, $b_i=z_i'(0)/\omega_i$ for $\lambda_i>0$ and $b_i=z_i'(0)$ for $\lambda_i=0$, so the displayed families cover every initial datum and are the complete solution sets for the first-order system $\bigl(z_i,z_i'\bigr)'=(z_i',-\lambda_iz_i)$;
3. consequently every solution of $Mq''+Kq=0$ is $q=M^{-1/2}Oz$ for a unique choice of the modal solutions of clause 2, and the correspondence between initial data $(q(0),q'(0))\in\mathbb R^{2n}$ and the coefficient tuples $(a_i,b_i)$ is a bijection;
4. for every solution the modal energies $E_i:=\tfrac12\bigl(z_i'^2+\lambda_iz_i^2\bigr)$ are constant on $I$, and so are

$$\tfrac12\dot q^{\mathsf T}M\dot q+\tfrac12q^{\mathsf T}Kq=\tfrac12|z'|_2^2+\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_iz_i^2=\sum_{i=1}^nE_i .$$

**(a) Data of a coupled quadratic model.** A **coupled quadratic model** (a
**quadratic oscillator model**) is declared by the following data: an integer
$n\ge1$, the number of **degrees of freedom**; a **mass metric matrix**
$M\in M_{n}(\mathbb R)$, symmetric and positive definite, that is
$M=M^{\mathsf T}$ and $v^{\mathsf T}Mv>0$ for every nonzero
$v\in\mathbb R^{n}$ ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); a **stiffness matrix**
$K\in M_{n}(\mathbb R)$, symmetric, $K=K^{\mathsf T}$; and an interval $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior
([[def-interval]]) together with a continuous **generalized force**
$J:I_{0}\to\mathbb R^{n}$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]).
When no force or time interval is prescribed, take $I_0:=\mathbb R$ and
$J(t):=0$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$; in particular this is the convention
for the small-oscillation model in clause (d).
The coordinates $q_{1},\dots,q_{n}$ of $\mathbb R^{n}$ are read in the chart
in which the model is declared and carry declared dimensions
$\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{n}$ and units, and time is read in seconds and mass
in kilograms ([[def-cm01-units]]). The data carry the dimensions

$$[M_{ij}]=\mu\ell^{2}\gamma_{i}^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1},\qquad [K_{ij}]=\mu\ell^{2}\gamma_{i}^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1}\tau^{-2},\qquad [J_{i}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}\gamma_{i}^{-1},$$

so that $\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}Mv$, $\tfrac12q^{\mathsf T}Kq$ and the pairing
$J\cdot\delta q$ of the generalized force with a coordinate variation all have
the energy dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; if the coordinate $q_{i}$ is
length-valued, $\gamma_{i}=\ell$, the entry $J_{i}$ has the force dimension
$\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. This is the dimension bookkeeping of a generalized
coordinate description in the sense of
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]], whose kinetic metric and
generalized forces are the framework objects the data present; the matrices
$M$ and $K$ are model parameters, not measured quantities.

**Fixed-unit numerical convention.** Choose a positive coordinate unit $s_i$ of dimension $\gamma_i$ for each direction, a time unit $t_*>0$ and an energy unit $e_*>0$, held fixed throughout a model calculation. Matrix products, square roots, eigenvectors, derivatives and Euclidean norms below act on numerical coefficients in these units, not on arrays of unlike physical quantities. Explicitly, if $Q_i$, $\mathsf M_{ij}$, $\mathsf K_{ij}$ and $\mathsf J_i$ denote the dimensional data, the symbols in the algebra are
$$q_i=Q_i/s_i,\qquad t=t_{\mathrm{phys}}/t_*,\qquad M_{ij}=\mathsf M_{ij}s_is_j/(e_*t_*^2),\qquad K_{ij}=\mathsf K_{ij}s_is_j/e_*,\qquad J_i=\mathsf J_i s_i/e_*.$$
Then $Mq''+Kq=J$ is exactly the physical equation in these coefficients, $Q_i=s_iq_i$, $\dot Q_i=(s_i/t_*)q_i'$, and the physical energy is $e_*E$. This is an invertible choice of units, imposing no restriction on the dimensions $\gamma_i$. For a variable metric and potential the same convention means $U(q)=U_{\mathrm{phys}}(s_1q_1,\ldots,s_nq_n)/e_*$ and $M_{ij}(q)=\mathsf M_{ij}(s_1q_1,\ldots,s_nq_n)s_is_j/(e_*t_*^2)$. Congruence by the positive diagonal coordinate-scale matrix and multiplication by positive constants preserve symmetry, definiteness and critical-point type.

**(b) Model equation, motions and phase system.** On any interval with
nonempty interior, $C^r$ for $r=1,2$ means that the first $r$ derivatives
exist and are continuous on that interval, using the domain-relative
derivative of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] at included
endpoints; on open intervals this agrees with
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The equation of the model
with data $(M,K,J)$ is

$$M\,q''(t)+K\,q(t)=J(t)\qquad(t\in I_{0}).$$

A **motion** of the model is a curve $q:J\to\mathbb R^{n}$ of class $C^{2}$
on an interval
$J\subseteq I_{0}$ with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) satisfying the
equation for every $t\in J$. A **datum** at $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is a pair
$(q_{0},v_{0})\in\mathbb R^{n}\times\mathbb R^{n}$. The **phase system** of
the model is the first-order linear system $z'=A z+b(t)$ on
$I_{0}\times\mathbb R^{2n}$ with $z=(q,v)$ and

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_{n}\\-M^{-1}K&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad b(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\M^{-1}J(t)\end{pmatrix},$$

where $M^{-1}$ is the inverse of $M$. By the product rule and invertibility of
$M$, a $C^{1}$ curve $t\mapsto(q(t),v(t))$ solves the phase system if and only
if $q$ is a motion of the model and $v=q'$. The model is **free** when
$J\equiv0$ and **forced, with generalized force $J$,** otherwise; the read of
$J$ as a prescribed external generalized force is the modelling status of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] for the external contributions
of a force model.

**(c) Quadratic energies and the mass metric.** The **kinetic energy**, the
**potential energy of the stiffness** and the **mechanical energy** of the
model are

$$T(v):=\tfrac12\,v^{\mathsf T}Mv,\qquad U_{K}(q):=\tfrac12\,q^{\mathsf T}Kq,\qquad E(q,v):=T(v)+U_{K}(q),$$

whose physical readings are $e_*$ times the displayed numerical quantities, all of energy dimension. $U_{K}$ is defined for every symmetric $K$; the name
records that $K$ is the matrix through which the model enters, and when $K$ is
indefinite $U_{K}$ is not non-negative, the model is not presented by a
potential with a local minimum at the origin, and no stability vocabulary is
attached to it by this item. The quadratic form $v\mapsto v^{\mathsf T}Mv$ is
positive definite and is called the **mass metric** of the model; the word
"metric" records only this positive-definiteness, and no distance on
configuration space is defined here.

**(d) Small-oscillation model at an equilibrium.** Let a mechanical system in
a chart be given by a $C^{2}$ field $q\mapsto G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q)$ of
symmetric positive definite matrices on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb
R^{n}$ and a $C^{2}$ potential $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$
([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]), and let
$q_{0}\in\Omega$ be a **mechanical equilibrium**, $\nabla U(q_{0})=0$. Its
**small-oscillation model at $q_{0}$** is the coupled quadratic model with
degrees of freedom $n$, mass metric matrix $M:=G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q_{0})$,
**stiffness matrix** $K_{0}:=D^{2}U(q_{0})$ — the Hessian of the potential
([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], symmetric by
[[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]]) — and zero generalized force, read in the
displacement coordinates $\xi:=q-q_{0}$. When the chart arises from the
generalized-coordinate dictionary of
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]], the matrix
$G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q_{0})=DX(q_{0})^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q_{0})$ is the
value at $q_{0}$ of that dictionary's kinetic metric. This clause assigns
model data to the equilibrium; the identification of the assigned model with
the derivative of the mechanical field, and every statement about its motions,
are separate results and are not asserted here.

**(e) Modal vocabulary of the decoupling data.** All the following matrix operations use the fixed-unit numerical convention. By clauses 1-3 of [[lem-cm-positive-definite-matrix-square-roots]], $M^{1/2}$ and its inverse $M^{-1/2}$ exist and are symmetric positive definite. For every symmetric $K$, without a sign restriction, $S:=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}$ is symmetric, since $S^{\mathsf T}=M^{-1/2}K^{\mathsf T}M^{-1/2}=S$. The [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] therefore supplies an orthogonal $O$ and real diagonal $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$ with $S=O\Lambda O^{\mathsf T}$. This construction includes negative eigenvalues; the restricted non-negative-$K$ result [[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]] is used only in that restricted case. Define **modal coordinates** $z:=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ and **modal vectors** $u_i:=M^{-1/2}Oe_i$, the columns of the inverse transform $q=M^{-1/2}Oz$. The **modal stiffnesses** are the real numbers $\lambda_i$. Direct multiplication gives $Ku_i=\lambda_iMu_i$ and $u_i^{\mathsf T}Mu_j=\delta_{ij}$. In physical units put $a_*:=\sqrt{e_*}\,t_*$. A modal coordinate has unit $a_*$; the $j$-th component of a mass-normalized modal vector has unit $s_j/a_*$, and the physical coordinate is the sum of the physical modal-vector components times their modal amplitudes. The matrix entries of $O$ and its orthonormal eigenvectors are dimensionless numerical coefficients. The physical modal stiffness is $\lambda_i/t_*^2$; an oscillatory or hyperbolic coefficient has unit $a_*$, while the slope coefficient in a zero-mode family $a_i+b_it$ has unit $a_*/t_*$. The physical frequency is $\sqrt{\lambda_i}/t_*$ when $\lambda_i>0$.

An index is **oscillatory** when $\lambda_i>0$, with numerical frequency $\omega_i:=\sqrt{\lambda_i}$; it is a **zero mode** when $\lambda_i=0$, and an **unstable (exponential) direction** when $\lambda_i<0$. Distinct indices are **degenerate** when their stiffnesses agree. For real $\lambda$ define the **modal eigenspace** $E_\lambda:=\ker(K-\lambda M)$. Its dimension is the multiplicity of $\lambda$, because $q\mapsto M^{1/2}q$ bijects it with the $\lambda$-eigenspace of $S$. The model is **oscillatory** when $K$ is non-negative. Indeed $x^{\mathsf T}Sx=(M^{-1/2}x)^{\mathsf T}K(M^{-1/2}x)$, so $K\ge0$ exactly when every $\lambda_i\ge0$; positive definiteness likewise corresponds to all $\lambda_i>0$. The zero-mode multiplicity is $\dim\ker K$. Frequencies are read in radians per unit time under [[def-cm01-units]].

**(f) Status.** This item introduces objects, vocabulary, domains, regularity
and dimensions for the restricted model class of this page and assigns its
small-oscillation model to a mechanical equilibrium. It contains no
existence, uniqueness, conservation, stability, resonance, degeneracy or
approximation assertion; those are proved on this page as separate items. It
adopts no force law of nature and records no measured value. Every later
statement of this page names the data $(M,K,J)$ or the mechanical data
$(G_{\mathrm{kin}},U,q_{0})$ it uses, and the one-dimensional instance is
recorded in the remarks.

Use the fixed coordinate, time and energy units and numerical matrix convention of [[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]]. Every displayed matrix identity and phase norm is in those numerical coordinates; physical positions, velocities, modal amplitudes, frequencies and energies are recovered by the stated fixed scale factors. This does not change the set of physical motions.

For real $u$, define the hyperbolic functions by
$\cosh u:=(e^{u}+e^{-u})/2$ and $\sinh u:=(e^{u}-e^{-u})/2$.

Global-time, growth and boundedness claims below refer to the unique maximal extension of the autonomous free equation on $\mathbb R$; local motions remain its restrictions. Values at $0$ in coefficient formulas are evaluated on that extension when the original interval omits $0$.

Adopt the free coupled quadratic model of
[[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]] with data $(M,K,J)$ in which
$J\equiv0$, $M$ is symmetric positive definite and $K$ is symmetric, with
modal data $M^{1/2}$, $M^{-1/2}$, $O$, $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n})$,
modal coordinates $z=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ and mode frequencies
$\omega_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}$ for $\lambda_{i}>0$. Write
$\kappa_{i}:=\sqrt{-\lambda_{i}}$ for $\lambda_{i}<0$. Then:

1. **Existence and uniqueness on the whole line.** For every $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$
and every datum $(q_{0},v_{0})\in\mathbb R^{2n}$ there is exactly one motion
$q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{n}$ with $q(t_{0})=q_{0}$ and $q'(t_{0})=v_{0}$; it
is the unique maximal motion through that datum.
2. **Complete modal classification.** A curve $q:J\to\mathbb R^{n}$ of class
$C^{2}$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a
motion of the free model if and only if its modal coordinates satisfy

$$z_{i}(t)=a_{i}\cos(\omega_{i}t)+b_{i}\sin(\omega_{i}t)\ (\lambda_{i}>0),\qquad z_{i}(t)=a_{i}+b_{i}t\ (\lambda_{i}=0),\qquad z_{i}(t)=a_{i}\cosh(\kappa_{i}t)+b_{i}\sinh(\kappa_{i}t)\ (\lambda_{i}<0)$$

for real numbers $a_{i},b_{i}$; the coefficients are unique and are
determined by the datum of the unique maximal extension through $a_{i}=z_{i}(0)$, $b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)/\omega_{i}$
for $\lambda_{i}>0$, $b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)$ for $\lambda_{i}=0$ and
$b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)/\kappa_{i}$ for $\lambda_{i}<0$.
3. **Energy and mode energies.** Along every motion the mechanical energy is
constant, and with $E_{i}:=\tfrac12\bigl(z_{i}'^{2}+\lambda_{i}z_{i}^{2}\bigr)$
one has $E(q,q')=\sum_{i=1}^{n}E_{i}$ and every $E_{i}$ is constant; for the
families of clause 2,

$$E_{i}=\tfrac12\omega_{i}^{2}\bigl(a_{i}^{2}+b_{i}^{2}\bigr)\ (\lambda_{i}>0),\qquad E_{i}=\tfrac12b_{i}^{2}\ (\lambda_{i}=0),\qquad E_{i}=\tfrac12\kappa_{i}^{2}\bigl(b_{i}^{2}-a_{i}^{2}\bigr)\ (\lambda_{i}<0).$$

4. **Degenerate families are intrinsic.** Let $\lambda$ be a modal stiffness,
let $E_{\lambda}^{S}:=\{u\in\mathbb R^{n}:M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}u=\lambda u\}$ and
let $N_{\lambda}:=M^{-1/2}E_{\lambda}^{S}$, a subspace of dimension equal to
the multiplicity of $\lambda$. A motion $q$ satisfies $z_{i}\equiv0$ for every
index $i$ with $\lambda_{i}\ne\lambda$ if and only if $q$ is a $C^{2}$ curve
with $q(t)\in N_{\lambda}$ for all $t$ in its interval and $q''+\lambda q=0$.
Consequently the family of such **pure-$\lambda$ motions** is independent of
the choice of diagonalization $O$: for $\lambda>0$ it consists exactly of
$q(t)=\cos(\omega t)q_{0}+\omega^{-1}\sin(\omega t)q_{1}$ with
$q_{0},q_{1}\in N_{\lambda}$ and $\omega=\sqrt{\lambda}$, for $\lambda=0$ of
$q(t)=q_{0}+tq_{1}$ with $q_{0},q_{1}\in N_{\lambda}$, and for $\lambda<0$ of
$q(t)=\cosh(\kappa t)q_{0}+\kappa^{-1}\sinh(\kappa t)q_{1}$ with
$\kappa=\sqrt{-\lambda}$. These formulas on a local interval are restrictions of their unique maximal extensions; $q_0,q_1$ are the position and velocity of that extension at time $0$, even if the local interval omits $0$. The individual modal vectors $u_{i}$ are not
intrinsic when the multiplicity exceeds one.
5. **Boundedness.** If $K$ is positive definite then every motion is bounded
on $\mathbb R$. If $K$ is non-negative and some $\lambda_{i}=0$, then a
motion with $z_{i}'\equiv b_{i}\ne0$ on a zero mode is unbounded on
$[0,\infty)$: the zero mode is affine, not oscillatory.
6. **Unstable direction.** If $K$ is not non-negative, then $(0,0)$ is not a
Lyapunov stable rest point of the free model
([[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]): there is $\varepsilon_{0}>0$
such that for every $\delta>0$ there are data with
$\lVert(q_{0},v_{0})\rVert_{2}<\delta$ whose motion reaches
$\lVert(q(t),q'(t))\rVert_{2}=\varepsilon_{0}$ at some time $t>0$.

The statement is read for the declared model data; no value of any parameter,
no physical realization and no measured frequency is asserted.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite matrices, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, let $q_0\in\Omega$ with $\nabla U(q_0)=0$, and suppose $q_0$ is a **strict local minimum** of $U$: there is $r_0>0$ with $\overline B(q_0,r_0)\subseteq\Omega$ and

$$U(q)>U(q_0)\qquad(0<\|q-q_0\|_2<r_0).$$

Let $G$ be the mechanical vector field of [[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]] on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$, with energy $E(q,v)=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v+U(q)$. Then $(q_0,0)$ is a Lyapunov stable equilibrium of $(q',v')=G(q,v)$ in the sense of [[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]: for every $\varepsilon>0$ with $\overline B((q_0,0),\varepsilon)\subseteq\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every maximal solution $(q,v)$ with $\|(q(0),v(0))-(q_0,0)\|_2<\delta$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies

$$\|(q(t),v(t))-(q_0,0)\|_2<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge0).$$

No asymptotic stability is asserted.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a map. Consider the autonomous first-order system

$$z'(t)=F(z(t)),$$

read as the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with $D=\mathbb R\times U$ and right-hand side $(t,z)\mapsto F(z)$. A **solution** below means a solution of this system on an interval containing $0$; a solution whose interval is $[0,\infty)$ or contains it is said to be **defined for all $t\ge0$**.

A solution $\tilde z:J\to U$ **extends** $z:I\to U$ when $I\subseteq J$ and $\tilde z|_I=z$; the extension is proper if $I\subsetneq J$. A solution is **maximal** when it has no proper extension ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]]). All stability predicates below quantify over maximal solutions whose intervals contain $0$; their local restrictions remain solutions. This convention asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of maximal solutions for an arbitrary map $F$.

A point $z_*\in U$ is an **equilibrium** (also **fixed point** or **zero**) of $F$ when $F(z_*)=0$; then the constant function $z(t)=z_*$ is a solution on every interval containing $0$.

Let $z_*\in U$ be an equilibrium.

1. $z_*$ is **Lyapunov stable** (or simply **stable**) when for every Euclidean ball $B_\varepsilon(z_*)$ with $\overline{B_\varepsilon(z_*)}\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) there is $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon]$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\|z(0)-z_*\|_2<\delta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies

$$\|z(t)-z_*\|_2<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge0).$$

2. $z_*$ is **asymptotically stable** when it is Lyapunov stable and in addition there is $\delta_0>0$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\|z(0)-z_*\|_2<\delta_0$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\|z(t)-z_*\|_2\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

An equilibrium which is not Lyapunov stable is **unstable**. An equilibrium is **globally asymptotically stable** when it is asymptotically stable and every maximal solution of the system is defined for all $t\ge0$ and converges to it as $t\to\infty$.

derivations.claim: Clause 1: by [F1] the stiffness $K=D^{2}U(q_{0})$ is symmetric and non-negative; by [F3] the small-oscillation model at $q_{0}$ is the coupled quadratic model with data $(M_{0},K,0)$, and a coupled quadratic model whose stiffness is non-negative is oscillatory in the sense of the definition's clause (e).

Clause 2: by [F2] the derivative of $G$ at $(q_{0},0)$ is $(\delta q,\delta v)\mapsto(\delta v,-M_{0}^{-1}K\delta q)$; by [F3] the phase system of the small-oscillation model is $y'=Ay$ for the same block matrix $A$, and the model equation $M_{0}\xi''+K\xi=0$ is equivalent to $(\xi,\xi')'=A(\xi,\xi')$ by the product rule and invertibility of $M_{0}$. This proves clause 2.

Clause 4: the hypotheses of [F5] are the $C^{2}$ positive definite metric field, the $C^{2}$ potential and the strict local minimum of the statement; its conclusion is exactly the Lyapunov stability assertion of clause 4 for the field $G$ and the rest point $(q_{0},0)$, whose equilibrium property is recorded in [[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]].

Clause 3: apply the classification of [F4] to the data $(M_{0},K,0)$ of the small-oscillation model; since $K$ is non-negative by [F1], every modal stiffness satisfies $\lambda_{i}\ge0$, so no exponential family occurs and the oscillatory and zero families of the free-mode theorem exhaust the motions, with frequencies $\omega_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}$ and the intrinsic pure-$\lambda$ families described there.

Clauses 1-4 are proved. Clause 4 is a nonlinear conclusion obtained from exact energy conservation, not from the linearization; clauses 2 and 3 describe the linearized model only, and no accuracy of that model as an approximation of the nonlinear motion, and no attraction, is claimed here.

boundaries.reason: Statement contains a specific equilibrium q0 and a positive-radius ball in its coordinate domain; the Hessian has the fixed positive dimension of that chart.

boundaries.evidence: Zero velocities and the zero displacement are included: the equilibrium point (q_0,0) and the zero curve at it are the base case of the statement, used in steps 1.1-1.3.
The scalar case n=1 is included: the statement is quantified over n≥1 and the stability conclusion of step 1.3 applies verbatim.
A degenerate strict minimum with a non-isolated flat direction is allowed: only strictness of the minimum is assumed and step 2.1 permits zero modal stiffnesses.
The stability statement is a forward-time statement (all t≥0) with no interval endpoint; the interval vocabulary is that of the maximal solutions used in step 1.3.

boundaries.reason: Step 1.1 uses the Hessian at the given minimum, and step 2.1 instantiates an existing modal decomposition. Stability comes from the already proved energy supplier, without choosing motions.

boundaries.evidence: Equivalence of the model equation with the linearized system: step 1.2 passes from the second-order model to the first-order block system.
Reverse direction of the equivalence: step 1.2 uses invertibility of M_0 to return from the block system to M_0 xi''+K xi=0.

risk_review.notes: Checked five steps: C2 metric/potential and interior strict minimum give symmetric semidefinite Hessian, not necessarily definite; derivative supplier matches mechanical field and small-oscillation phase system. Free model defaults to all R; both motion/phase directions hold. Zero Hessian remains allowed, e.g. q^4; nonlinear stability comes from exact energy supplier and compact trapping, whose proof was opened, not from linear modes. No attraction, all-time approximation, or empirical frequency asserted.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $M(q)$ symmetric and positive definite for every $q\in\Omega$, that is $v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$. The matrix field $M$ is the **kinetic metric field** and $U$ the **potential** of the data in the chart $\Omega$.

Define, for $(q,v)\in\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$, the **kinetic energy**, **Lagrangian** and **energy**

$$T(q,v):=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v,\qquad L(q,v):=T(q,v)-U(q),\qquad E(q,v):=T(q,v)+U(q),$$

and, for $q\in\Omega$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the matrix

$$D_qM(q)[v]:=\sum_{k=1}^nv_k\,\partial_kM(q),\qquad\bigl(\partial_kM(q)\bigr)_{ij}=\partial_kM_{ij}(q).$$

The **mechanical vector field** of the data is the map

$$G:\Omega\times\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n,\qquad G(q,v)=\Bigl(v,\ M(q)^{-1}\bigl(\tfrac12\nabla_q(v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v)-\bigl(D_qM(q)[v]\bigr)v-\nabla U(q)\bigr)\Bigr),$$

where $\nabla_q$ and $\nabla U$ are Euclidean gradients ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and $M(q)^{-1}$ is the inverse of the positive definite matrix $M(q)$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]], [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). The **mechanical system** in the chart is the first-order system

$$q'(t)=v(t),\qquad v'(t)=M(q(t))^{-1}\Bigl(\tfrac12\nabla_qf\bigl(q(t),v(t)\bigr)-\bigl(D_qM(q(t))[v(t)]\bigr)v(t)-\nabla U(q(t))\Bigr),\qquad f(q,v):=v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v .$$

A point $q_* \in\Omega$ is a **mechanical equilibrium** when $\nabla U(q_*)=0$.

If $R$ is a commutative ring, $n\geq1$, $A\in M_n(R)$, and $\det(A)$ is a
unit, then

$$A^{-1}=\det(A)^{-1}\operatorname{adj}(A).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $F$ is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniformly in time**, if every compact time-state cylinder $C\subseteq D$ has a finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x),(t,y)\in C$ have the same time coordinate.

On every compact time-state cylinder the state-variable inequality holds with one finite constant $L$. More generally, let $p\ge1$, let $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R^p$, let $D_\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\Lambda$ be open in its relative Euclidean topology, and let $F:D_\Lambda\to\mathbb R^n$. The parameter family is **locally Lipschitz in the state variable, locally uniform in time and parameters** when every compact time-state-parameter cylinder $C\subseteq D_\Lambda$ has one finite $L\ge0$ such that

$$\|F(t,x,\lambda)-F(t,y,\lambda)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$$

whenever $(t,x,\lambda),(t,y,\lambda)\in C$ have the same time and parameter coordinates.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^2$ field of symmetric positive definite matrices, let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, and let $q_0\in\Omega$ be a mechanical equilibrium, that is $\nabla U(q_0)=0$ ([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]). Let $G$ be the mechanical vector field on $\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$. Then:

1. $G$ is totally differentiable at $(q_0,0)$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]]) and, writing $D^2U(q_0)$ for the Hessian matrix ([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]),

$$DG(q_0,0)(\delta q,\delta v)=\Bigl(\delta v,\ -M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)\,\delta q\Bigr)\qquad(\delta q,\delta v\in\mathbb R^n);$$

2. consequently the linearised equation at the equilibrium is

$$\xi''=-M(q_0)^{-1}D^2U(q_0)\,\xi,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad M(q_0)\xi''+D^2U(q_0)\,\xi=0,$$

a constant-coefficient system whose mass matrix $M(q_0)$ is symmetric positive definite and whose stiffness matrix $D^2U(q_0)$ is symmetric ([[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]]);
3. if in addition $q_0$ is a strict local minimum of $U$, then $K:=D^2U(q_0)$ is non-negative, so the hypotheses of [[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]] are satisfied by $M(q_0)$ and $K$, and the linearised system is exactly the constant-coefficient quadratic system of that theorem with mass matrix $M(q_0)$ and stiffness $K$; its modes are the normal modes of the linearisation.
For a $C^2$ scalar field $f$, $H_f(a)^T=H_f(a)$ at every point $a$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$,
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]],
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]). Let
$M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $M \ge 0$ satisfy

$$\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } t \in (a,b).$$

Then

$$\lVert f(b) - f(a)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,(b-a).$$

**No integrability of $f'$ is assumed**, so the theorem applies to every
differentiable $f$; that is why it is proved from the scalar mean value theorem
rather than from
[[thm-norm-inequality-for-the-vector-valued-integral]].
[[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]] records the comparison between the
two routes.

**The equality form is not asserted, and for $m \ge 2$ it is false.** There need
be **no** $\xi \in (a,b)$ with $f(b)-f(a) = f'(\xi)(b-a)$; the companion page
carries a differentiable witness on $[0,1]$. The $\xi$ produced in the proof
below depends on the fixed vector $u = f(b)-f(a)$ and is a mean value point of
the **real** function $t \mapsto \langle u, f(t)\rangle$, not of $f$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $0\in U$, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $r>0$, $C\ge0$, $L\ge0$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\overline B(0,r)\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) and

$$\|F(z)-Az\|_2\le C\|z\|_2^2,\qquad \|F(z)\|_2\le L\|z\|_2\qquad(\|z\|_2\le r),$$
where $Az$ and $\|A\|$ use the matrix-action and induced Euclidean operator-norm convention of [[cor-cm-variation-of-constants-for-linear-systems]].

Let $z_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $\delta:=\|z_0\|_2>0$, let $T>0$ with $\delta e^{LT}<r$, and let $y:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be the solution of the linear system $y'=Ay$, $y(0)=z_0$ ([[cor-cm-variation-of-constants-for-linear-systems]]). Then:

1. The maximal solution $z$ of $z'=F(z)$, $z(0)=z_0$ is defined on $[0,T]$ and satisfies $\|z(t)\|_2\le\delta e^{Lt}$ for $t\in[0,T]$ ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]]).
2. For every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|z(t)-y(t)\|_2\le C\delta^2\int_0^te^{\|A\|(t-s)}e^{2Ls}\,ds\le C\delta^2\,t\,e^{(\|A\|+2L)t},$$
where $\|A\|$ is the operator norm of $A$ for the Euclidean norm ([[def-operator-norm]]).

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ and $y:J\to\mathbb R^n$ solve the same IVP. The solution $y$ is an **extension** of $x$ when $I\subseteq J$ and $y|_I=x$. It is a proper extension when $I\subsetneq J$.

A solution is **maximal** when it has no proper extension. Its domain is its **maximal interval of existence**. A solution is **global** when its domain is the entire time projection allowed by the ODE domain; for a vector field on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$, this means domain $\mathbb R$.

**(a) Data of a coupled quadratic model.** A **coupled quadratic model** (a
**quadratic oscillator model**) is declared by the following data: an integer
$n\ge1$, the number of **degrees of freedom**; a **mass metric matrix**
$M\in M_{n}(\mathbb R)$, symmetric and positive definite, that is
$M=M^{\mathsf T}$ and $v^{\mathsf T}Mv>0$ for every nonzero
$v\in\mathbb R^{n}$ ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); a **stiffness matrix**
$K\in M_{n}(\mathbb R)$, symmetric, $K=K^{\mathsf T}$; and an interval $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior
([[def-interval]]) together with a continuous **generalized force**
$J:I_{0}\to\mathbb R^{n}$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]).
When no force or time interval is prescribed, take $I_0:=\mathbb R$ and
$J(t):=0$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$; in particular this is the convention
for the small-oscillation model in clause (d).
The coordinates $q_{1},\dots,q_{n}$ of $\mathbb R^{n}$ are read in the chart
in which the model is declared and carry declared dimensions
$\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{n}$ and units, and time is read in seconds and mass
in kilograms ([[def-cm01-units]]). The data carry the dimensions

$$[M_{ij}]=\mu\ell^{2}\gamma_{i}^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1},\qquad [K_{ij}]=\mu\ell^{2}\gamma_{i}^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1}\tau^{-2},\qquad [J_{i}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}\gamma_{i}^{-1},$$

so that $\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}Mv$, $\tfrac12q^{\mathsf T}Kq$ and the pairing
$J\cdot\delta q$ of the generalized force with a coordinate variation all have
the energy dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; if the coordinate $q_{i}$ is
length-valued, $\gamma_{i}=\ell$, the entry $J_{i}$ has the force dimension
$\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. This is the dimension bookkeeping of a generalized
coordinate description in the sense of
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]], whose kinetic metric and
generalized forces are the framework objects the data present; the matrices
$M$ and $K$ are model parameters, not measured quantities.

**Fixed-unit numerical convention.** Choose a positive coordinate unit $s_i$ of dimension $\gamma_i$ for each direction, a time unit $t_*>0$ and an energy unit $e_*>0$, held fixed throughout a model calculation. Matrix products, square roots, eigenvectors, derivatives and Euclidean norms below act on numerical coefficients in these units, not on arrays of unlike physical quantities. Explicitly, if $Q_i$, $\mathsf M_{ij}$, $\mathsf K_{ij}$ and $\mathsf J_i$ denote the dimensional data, the symbols in the algebra are
$$q_i=Q_i/s_i,\qquad t=t_{\mathrm{phys}}/t_*,\qquad M_{ij}=\mathsf M_{ij}s_is_j/(e_*t_*^2),\qquad K_{ij}=\mathsf K_{ij}s_is_j/e_*,\qquad J_i=\mathsf J_i s_i/e_*.$$
Then $Mq''+Kq=J$ is exactly the physical equation in these coefficients, $Q_i=s_iq_i$, $\dot Q_i=(s_i/t_*)q_i'$, and the physical energy is $e_*E$. This is an invertible choice of units, imposing no restriction on the dimensions $\gamma_i$. For a variable metric and potential the same convention means $U(q)=U_{\mathrm{phys}}(s_1q_1,\ldots,s_nq_n)/e_*$ and $M_{ij}(q)=\mathsf M_{ij}(s_1q_1,\ldots,s_nq_n)s_is_j/(e_*t_*^2)$. Congruence by the positive diagonal coordinate-scale matrix and multiplication by positive constants preserve symmetry, definiteness and critical-point type.

**(b) Model equation, motions and phase system.** On any interval with
nonempty interior, $C^r$ for $r=1,2$ means that the first $r$ derivatives
exist and are continuous on that interval, using the domain-relative
derivative of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] at included
endpoints; on open intervals this agrees with
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The equation of the model
with data $(M,K,J)$ is

$$M\,q''(t)+K\,q(t)=J(t)\qquad(t\in I_{0}).$$

A **motion** of the model is a curve $q:J\to\mathbb R^{n}$ of class $C^{2}$
on an interval
$J\subseteq I_{0}$ with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) satisfying the
equation for every $t\in J$. A **datum** at $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is a pair
$(q_{0},v_{0})\in\mathbb R^{n}\times\mathbb R^{n}$. The **phase system** of
the model is the first-order linear system $z'=A z+b(t)$ on
$I_{0}\times\mathbb R^{2n}$ with $z=(q,v)$ and

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_{n}\\-M^{-1}K&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad b(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\M^{-1}J(t)\end{pmatrix},$$

where $M^{-1}$ is the inverse of $M$. By the product rule and invertibility of
$M$, a $C^{1}$ curve $t\mapsto(q(t),v(t))$ solves the phase system if and only
if $q$ is a motion of the model and $v=q'$. The model is **free** when
$J\equiv0$ and **forced, with generalized force $J$,** otherwise; the read of
$J$ as a prescribed external generalized force is the modelling status of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] for the external contributions
of a force model.

**(c) Quadratic energies and the mass metric.** The **kinetic energy**, the
**potential energy of the stiffness** and the **mechanical energy** of the
model are

$$T(v):=\tfrac12\,v^{\mathsf T}Mv,\qquad U_{K}(q):=\tfrac12\,q^{\mathsf T}Kq,\qquad E(q,v):=T(v)+U_{K}(q),$$

whose physical readings are $e_*$ times the displayed numerical quantities, all of energy dimension. $U_{K}$ is defined for every symmetric $K$; the name
records that $K$ is the matrix through which the model enters, and when $K$ is
indefinite $U_{K}$ is not non-negative, the model is not presented by a
potential with a local minimum at the origin, and no stability vocabulary is
attached to it by this item. The quadratic form $v\mapsto v^{\mathsf T}Mv$ is
positive definite and is called the **mass metric** of the model; the word
"metric" records only this positive-definiteness, and no distance on
configuration space is defined here.

**(d) Small-oscillation model at an equilibrium.** Let a mechanical system in
a chart be given by a $C^{2}$ field $q\mapsto G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q)$ of
symmetric positive definite matrices on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb
R^{n}$ and a $C^{2}$ potential $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$
([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]), and let
$q_{0}\in\Omega$ be a **mechanical equilibrium**, $\nabla U(q_{0})=0$. Its
**small-oscillation model at $q_{0}$** is the coupled quadratic model with
degrees of freedom $n$, mass metric matrix $M:=G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q_{0})$,
**stiffness matrix** $K_{0}:=D^{2}U(q_{0})$ — the Hessian of the potential
([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], symmetric by
[[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]]) — and zero generalized force, read in the
displacement coordinates $\xi:=q-q_{0}$. When the chart arises from the
generalized-coordinate dictionary of
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]], the matrix
$G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q_{0})=DX(q_{0})^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q_{0})$ is the
value at $q_{0}$ of that dictionary's kinetic metric. This clause assigns
model data to the equilibrium; the identification of the assigned model with
the derivative of the mechanical field, and every statement about its motions,
are separate results and are not asserted here.

**(e) Modal vocabulary of the decoupling data.** All the following matrix operations use the fixed-unit numerical convention. By clauses 1-3 of [[lem-cm-positive-definite-matrix-square-roots]], $M^{1/2}$ and its inverse $M^{-1/2}$ exist and are symmetric positive definite. For every symmetric $K$, without a sign restriction, $S:=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}$ is symmetric, since $S^{\mathsf T}=M^{-1/2}K^{\mathsf T}M^{-1/2}=S$. The [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] therefore supplies an orthogonal $O$ and real diagonal $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$ with $S=O\Lambda O^{\mathsf T}$. This construction includes negative eigenvalues; the restricted non-negative-$K$ result [[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]] is used only in that restricted case. Define **modal coordinates** $z:=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ and **modal vectors** $u_i:=M^{-1/2}Oe_i$, the columns of the inverse transform $q=M^{-1/2}Oz$. The **modal stiffnesses** are the real numbers $\lambda_i$. Direct multiplication gives $Ku_i=\lambda_iMu_i$ and $u_i^{\mathsf T}Mu_j=\delta_{ij}$. In physical units put $a_*:=\sqrt{e_*}\,t_*$. A modal coordinate has unit $a_*$; the $j$-th component of a mass-normalized modal vector has unit $s_j/a_*$, and the physical coordinate is the sum of the physical modal-vector components times their modal amplitudes. The matrix entries of $O$ and its orthonormal eigenvectors are dimensionless numerical coefficients. The physical modal stiffness is $\lambda_i/t_*^2$; an oscillatory or hyperbolic coefficient has unit $a_*$, while the slope coefficient in a zero-mode family $a_i+b_it$ has unit $a_*/t_*$. The physical frequency is $\sqrt{\lambda_i}/t_*$ when $\lambda_i>0$.

An index is **oscillatory** when $\lambda_i>0$, with numerical frequency $\omega_i:=\sqrt{\lambda_i}$; it is a **zero mode** when $\lambda_i=0$, and an **unstable (exponential) direction** when $\lambda_i<0$. Distinct indices are **degenerate** when their stiffnesses agree. For real $\lambda$ define the **modal eigenspace** $E_\lambda:=\ker(K-\lambda M)$. Its dimension is the multiplicity of $\lambda$, because $q\mapsto M^{1/2}q$ bijects it with the $\lambda$-eigenspace of $S$. The model is **oscillatory** when $K$ is non-negative. Indeed $x^{\mathsf T}Sx=(M^{-1/2}x)^{\mathsf T}K(M^{-1/2}x)$, so $K\ge0$ exactly when every $\lambda_i\ge0$; positive definiteness likewise corresponds to all $\lambda_i>0$. The zero-mode multiplicity is $\dim\ker K$. Frequencies are read in radians per unit time under [[def-cm01-units]].

**(f) Status.** This item introduces objects, vocabulary, domains, regularity
and dimensions for the restricted model class of this page and assigns its
small-oscillation model to a mechanical equilibrium. It contains no
existence, uniqueness, conservation, stability, resonance, degeneracy or
approximation assertion; those are proved on this page as separate items. It
adopts no force law of nature and records no measured value. Every later
statement of this page names the data $(M,K,J)$ or the mechanical data
$(G_{\mathrm{kin}},U,q_{0})$ it uses, and the one-dimensional instance is
recorded in the remarks.

derivations.claim: Clauses 1 and the derivative identity: by [F1] the translated field $F$ is $C^{2}$ on its open domain and locally Lipschitz; $F(0)=0$ and $A=DF(0)=DG(q_{0},0)$ with the displayed block form are [F2].

Quantitative remainder and growth bounds: since $F$ is $C^{2}$, $DF$ is $C^{1}$, hence continuous on the compact ball $\overline B(0,r_{0})$; thus $L:=\sup_{\lVert\eta\rVert_{2}\le r_{0}}\lVert DF(\eta)\rVert$ is finite, and $DF$ is Lipschitz on the convex ball with some finite constant $\Lambda$ (each entry of $DF$ has continuous gradient and is Lipschitz on the ball by [F3] with the supremum of that gradient; a finite sum of such bounds bounds $\lVert DF(\eta)-DF(\eta')\rVert$). For $\lVert\zeta\rVert_{2}\le r_{0}$, [F4] applied to the $C^{1}$ curve $t\mapsto F(t\zeta)-tA\zeta$, whose derivative is $DF(t\zeta)\zeta-A\zeta=(DF(t\zeta)-DF(0))\zeta$, gives $$F(\zeta)-A\zeta=\int_{0}^{1}\bigl(DF(t\zeta)-DF(0)\bigr)\zeta\,dt,$$ hence $\lVert F(\zeta)-A\zeta\rVert_{2}\le\int_{0}^{1}\Lambda t\lVert\zeta\rVert_{2}^{2}dt=\tfrac{\Lambda}{2}\lVert\zeta\rVert_{2}^{2}$; and $F(\zeta)=F(\zeta)-F(0)$ with [F3] gives $\lVert F(\zeta)\rVert_{2}\le L\lVert\zeta\rVert_{2}$. This proves the bounds of clause 1 with $C=\Lambda/2$.

The finite-time bound: apply [F5] to $F$, the constants $r_{0},C,L$, the matrix $A$ and the displaced datum $\zeta_0=(\delta q_0,v_0)$ of norm $\delta$. The maximal solution $\zeta$ of $\zeta'=F(\zeta)$ is defined on $[0,T]$ and obeys the error bound against $\widetilde y$. Translating back gives $z(t)=(q_0+\zeta_q(t),\zeta_v(t))$, the physical phase solution through $z_0$; $y(t)=(q_0+\xi(t),\eta(t))$ has exactly the same translation, so $\|z(t)-y(t)\|_2=\|\zeta(t)-\widetilde y(t)\|_2$; this is clause 2.

Identification of the linear solution: by [F2] the matrix $A$ is the block matrix $(\delta q,\delta v)\mapsto(\delta v,-M(q_{0})^{-1}D^{2}U(q_{0})\delta q)$; the displacement linear solution $\widetilde y=(\xi,\eta)$ of $\widetilde y'=A\widetilde y$, $\widetilde y(0)=(\delta q_0,v_0)$ therefore satisfies $\eta=\xi'$, hence $\xi''=-M(q_{0})^{-1}D^{2}U(q_{0})\xi$, equivalently $M(q_{0})\xi''+D^{2}U(q_{0})\xi=0$, with $\xi(0)=\delta q_{0}$, $\xi'(0)=v_{0}$; by [F6] this is exactly the motion of the small-oscillation model with that datum, and it is unique by the model's phase-system uniqueness. This is clause 3.

Clauses 1-3 are proved. The estimate is a finite-time statement under the explicit smallness hypothesis $\delta e^{LT}<r_{0}$; the constants $C,L$ exist by compactness and are not asserted to be optimal, and no long-time, stability or empirical conclusion is drawn.

boundaries.reason: The positive-dimensional chart contains q0 and its closed radius-r0 ball. Step 1.2 bounds derivatives on this nonempty compact ball; no empty supremum is taken.

boundaries.evidence: The zero displacement at the equilibrium gives F(0)=0 and the zero-datum case is excluded by delta>0 only to avoid a trivial normalization; the constants of step 1.2 are finite also at zero.
The one-dimensional case n=1 is included; the statement is quantified over every n≥1 and the state dimension 2n is named in [F5].

boundaries.reason: No rank, invertibility or distinctness hypothesis degenerates in the statement: M is positive definite on the ball, so no eigenvalue condition arises.

boundaries.evidence: The horizon endpoints are explicit: the estimate holds on the closed interval [0,T] under delta e^{LT}<r_0, as used in step 2.1.

Let $n\ge1$, let $M\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric positive definite, let $K\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric and non-negative, let $S:=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}=O\Lambda O^{\mathsf T}$ with $O$ orthogonal and $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$, $\lambda_i\ge0$ ([[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and let $t_0\in I$. Put

$$\psi(t):=O^{\mathsf T}M^{-1/2}\varphi(t),\qquad \omega_i:=\sqrt{\lambda_i}\ (\lambda_i>0),$$

and for a curve $q:I\to\mathbb R^n$ whose first and second derivatives exist on $I$ (relative to $I$ at included endpoints) and whose second derivative is continuous on $I$, put $z:=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$. Then:

1. $q$ solves the forced quadratic system $Mq''+Kq=\varphi$ on $I$ if and only if $z$ solves the decoupled forced system
$$z_i''+\lambda_iz_i=\psi_i\qquad(1\le i\le n)$$
on $I$.
2. For each $i$, the unique solution $z_i:I\to\mathbb R$ of the scalar equation in clause 1 with data $z_i(t_0)=\xi_i$, $z_i'(t_0)=\eta_i$ is
$$z_i(t)=\xi_i\cos\bigl(\omega_i(t-t_0)\bigr)+\frac{\eta_i}{\omega_i}\sin\bigl(\omega_i(t-t_0)\bigr)+\frac1{\omega_i}\int_{t_0}^t\sin\bigl(\omega_i(t-s)\bigr)\psi_i(s)\,ds\quad(\lambda_i>0),$$
$$z_i(t)=\xi_i+\eta_i(t-t_0)+\int_{t_0}^t(t-s)\psi_i(s)\,ds\quad(\lambda_i=0).$$
3. Consequently, for every initial datum $(q(t_0),q'(t_0))\in\mathbb R^{2n}$ there is exactly one solution $q:I\to\mathbb R^n$ of $Mq''+Kq=\varphi$ with that datum, and it is $q=M^{-1/2}Oz$ for the $z$ of clause 2.

Let $m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$, let $f_0\in\mathbb R$ and $\Omega\ge0$, and consider the forced model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f$ with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(t)=f_0\cos(\Omega t)$ ([[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]). Put

$$D:=k-m\Omega^2+i\,c\,\Omega\in\mathbb C,\qquad \omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}.$$

1. **Non-resonant response.** If $D\ne0$, then the function
$$x_p(t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\frac{f_0e^{i\Omega t}}{D}\right)=f_0\,\frac{(k-m\Omega^2)\cos(\Omega t)+c\,\Omega\sin(\Omega t)}{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}$$
is a solution of the forced model on all of $\mathbb R$. Its amplitude about zero is $|f_0|/\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}$.

2. **Resonance.** If $c=0$ and $\Omega=\omega_0$, then $D=0$ and
$$x_p(t):=\frac{f_0\,t\sin(\omega_0t)}{2m\omega_0}$$
is a solution of the forced model on all of $\mathbb R$; if $f_0\ne0$ then $x_p$ is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$.

3. **Transient decay.** If $c>0$, then $D\ne0$ for every $\Omega\ge0$, and every solution $x:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ of the forced model satisfies
$$x(t)=x_p(t)+x_h(t)$$
where $x_h$ is a homogeneous solution; consequently $x(t)-x_p(t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$ ([[def-limits-at-infinity]]) and $x$ is bounded on $[0,\infty)$.
