$J\subseteq I_{0}$ with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) satisfying the
equation for every $t\in J$. A **datum** at $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is a pair
$(q_{0},v_{0})\in\mathbb R^{n}\times\mathbb R^{n}$. The **phase system** of
the model is the first-order linear system $z'=A z+b(t)$ on
$I_{0}\times\mathbb R^{2n}$ with $z=(q,v)$ and

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_{n}\\-M^{-1}K&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad b(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\M^{-1}J(t)\end{pmatrix},$$

where $M^{-1}$ is the inverse of $M$. By the product rule and invertibility of
$M$, a $C^{1}$ curve $t\mapsto(q(t),v(t))$ solves the phase system if and only
if $q$ is a motion of the model and $v=q'$. The model is **free** when
$J\equiv0$ and **forced, with generalized force $J$,** otherwise; the read of
$J$ as a prescribed external generalized force is the modelling status of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] for the external contributions
of a force model.

**(c) Quadratic energies and the mass metric.** The **kinetic energy**, the
**potential energy of the stiffness** and the **mechanical energy** of the
model are

$$T(v):=\tfrac12\,v^{\mathsf T}Mv,\qquad U_{K}(q):=\tfrac12\,q^{\mathsf T}Kq,\qquad E(q,v):=T(v)+U_{K}(q),$$

whose physical readings are $e_*$ times the displayed numerical quantities, all of energy dimension. $U_{K}$ is defined for every symmetric $K$; the name
records that $K$ is the matrix through which the model enters, and when $K$ is
indefinite $U_{K}$ is not non-negative, the model is not presented by a
potential with a local minimum at the origin, and no stability vocabulary is
attached to it by this item. The quadratic form $v\mapsto v^{\mathsf T}Mv$ is
positive definite and is called the **mass metric** of the model; the word
"metric" records only this positive-definiteness, and no distance on
configuration space is defined here.

**(d) Small-oscillation model at an equilibrium.** Let a mechanical system in
a chart be given by a $C^{2}$ field $q\mapsto G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q)$ of
symmetric positive definite matrices on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb
R^{n}$ and a $C^{2}$ potential $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$
([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]), and let
$q_{0}\in\Omega$ be a **mechanical equilibrium**, $\nabla U(q_{0})=0$. Its
**small-oscillation model at $q_{0}$** is the coupled quadratic model with
degrees of freedom $n$, mass metric matrix $M:=G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q_{0})$,
**stiffness matrix** $K_{0}:=D^{2}U(q_{0})$ — the Hessian of the potential
([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], symmetric by
[[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]]) — and zero generalized force, read in the
displacement coordinates $\xi:=q-q_{0}$. When the chart arises from the
generalized-coordinate dictionary of
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]], the matrix
$G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q_{0})=DX(q_{0})^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q_{0})$ is the
value at $q_{0}$ of that dictionary's kinetic metric. This clause assigns
model data to the equilibrium; the identification of the assigned model with
the derivative of the mechanical field, and every statement about its motions,
are separate results and are not asserted here.

**(e) Modal vocabulary of the decoupling data.** All the following matrix operations use the fixed-unit numerical convention. By clauses 1-3 of [[lem-cm-positive-definite-matrix-square-roots]], $M^{1/2}$ and its inverse $M^{-1/2}$ exist and are symmetric positive definite. For every symmetric $K$, without a sign restriction, $S:=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}$ is symmetric, since $S^{\mathsf T}=M^{-1/2}K^{\mathsf T}M^{-1/2}=S$. The [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] therefore supplies an orthogonal $O$ and real diagonal $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$ with $S=O\Lambda O^{\mathsf T}$. This construction includes negative eigenvalues; the restricted non-negative-$K$ result [[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]] is used only in that restricted case. Define **modal coordinates** $z:=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ and **modal vectors** $u_i:=M^{-1/2}Oe_i$, the columns of the inverse transform $q=M^{-1/2}Oz$. The **modal stiffnesses** are the real numbers $\lambda_i$. Direct multiplication gives $Ku_i=\lambda_iMu_i$ and $u_i^{\mathsf T}Mu_j=\delta_{ij}$. In physical units put $a_*:=\sqrt{e_*}\,t_*$. A modal coordinate has unit $a_*$; the $j$-th component of a mass-normalized modal vector has unit $s_j/a_*$, and the physical coordinate is the sum of the physical modal-vector components times their modal amplitudes. The matrix entries of $O$ and its orthonormal eigenvectors are dimensionless numerical coefficients. The physical modal stiffness is $\lambda_i/t_*^2$; an oscillatory or hyperbolic coefficient has unit $a_*$, while the slope coefficient in a zero-mode family $a_i+b_it$ has unit $a_*/t_*$. The physical frequency is $\sqrt{\lambda_i}/t_*$ when $\lambda_i>0$.

An index is **oscillatory** when $\lambda_i>0$, with numerical frequency $\omega_i:=\sqrt{\lambda_i}$; it is a **zero mode** when $\lambda_i=0$, and an **unstable (exponential) direction** when $\lambda_i<0$. Distinct indices are **degenerate** when their stiffnesses agree. For real $\lambda$ define the **modal eigenspace** $E_\lambda:=\ker(K-\lambda M)$. Its dimension is the multiplicity of $\lambda$, because $q\mapsto M^{1/2}q$ bijects it with the $\lambda$-eigenspace of $S$. The model is **oscillatory** when $K$ is non-negative. Indeed $x^{\mathsf T}Sx=(M^{-1/2}x)^{\mathsf T}K(M^{-1/2}x)$, so $K\ge0$ exactly when every $\lambda_i\ge0$; positive definiteness likewise corresponds to all $\lambda_i>0$. The zero-mode multiplicity is $\dim\ker K$. Frequencies are read in radians per unit time under [[def-cm01-units]].

**(f) Status.** This item introduces objects, vocabulary, domains, regularity
and dimensions for the restricted model class of this page and assigns its
small-oscillation model to a mechanical equilibrium. It contains no
existence, uniqueness, conservation, stability, resonance, degeneracy or
approximation assertion; those are proved on this page as separate items. It
adopts no force law of nature and records no measured value. Every later
statement of this page names the data $(M,K,J)$ or the mechanical data
$(G_{\mathrm{kin}},U,q_{0})$ it uses, and the one-dimensional instance is
recorded in the remarks.

**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, mass $m>0$, spring
constant $k>0$ ([[post-cm04-harmonic-model]]) and drag coefficient $c\ge0$
([[post-cm04-linear-damping-model]]). Let a real **drive amplitude**
$f_{0}\in\mathbb R$ of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ (newtons) and an
**angular drive frequency** $\Omega>0$ of dimension $\tau^{-1}$ (radians per
second; the radian is dimensionless in the framework's angle convention,
[[def-cm01-units]]) be declared. Adopt, through the additive composition of
force contributions of clause (v) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and
the external-contribution reading of [[post-cm02-interactions]], the force
law
$$F(t,x,v):=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)-k\,x-c\,v .$$
The **sinusoidally driven oscillator model** is the one-dimensional model
with this force law; its equation of motion is
$$m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t),$$
and its data $(m,c,k,f)$ with $f(t)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$ are oscillator-type
data in the sense of clause (f) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]. The term
$f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$ is the **drive** or **driving force**; the model is
undamped when $c=0$ and strictly damped when $c>0$.

**(ii) The drive is prescribed external data.** The driving force is a
prescribed function of time alone: it does not depend on $x$ or on $x'$, and
the object producing it is not one of the model's labels and is not modelled
dynamically. This is the same modelling status as the medium of
[[post-cm02-drag]]: the drive is an external contribution declared as part
of the model. A real apparatus, background or force generator that reacts to
the motion is **not** represented by this model; representing such a
back-reaction requires a larger model with additional states.

**(iii) Potential presentation with residual force.** The model presents its
force law through the harmonic potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$ with residual
force $d(t,x,v)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)-c\,v$, in the sense of clause (d) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$F(t,x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)$. The mechanical energy of the model is
$E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$ of that clause, defined along every
motion; the model is driven and not a global potential model whenever
$f_{0}\neq0$.

**(iv) Regularity.** Let $X:=x_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$,
$V:=v_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$, and $T:=t_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm s)$
be the dimensionless numerical SI coordinates (the real inputs of the force
map). Write
$K:=k_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{N/m})$,
$C:=c_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{kg/s})$,
$\widehat f_{0}:=f_{0}/(1\,\mathrm N)$, and
$\widehat\Omega:=\Omega(1\,\mathrm s)$. The numerical force map is
$$\widehat F(T,X,V)=\widehat f_{0}\cos(\widehat\Omega T)-KX-CV,$$
so it is continuous and globally Lipschitz in the state variable with
numerical-coordinate constant $K+C$, uniformly in time. This is a bound on
dimensionless SI coordinates and force values, not a sum of the dimensionful
$k$ and $c$ ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). It is an
admissible force law of clause (a) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]],
and its equation is the forced model $m\,x''+cx'+kx=f$ of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with the continuous function
$f(t)=f_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$.

**(v) Physical status and regime.** The model is a **restricted idealization**
adopted rather than derived: exactly sinusoidal, with constant amplitude and
frequency and no dependence on the motion. The drive amplitude and frequency
are model parameters; when their values come from an apparatus calibration,
that use is an empirical premise carrying the apparatus conditions and the
measurement uncertainty, and this item asserts no such value. The sinusoidal
form is the elementary component used by the recorded treatments; the
response to a non-sinusoidal periodic drive is a superposition statement
belonging to the mathematical theory, not an additional claim here. The
model's undamped case $c=0$ is included as a parameter value, and it is where
the resonant unboundedness of the following theorem occurs.

**(vi) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes
it; it selects no law of nature on its own, and no measured response, no
resonance curve of any apparatus and no empirical resonance phenomenon is
asserted by the postulate.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k\in\mathbb R$ be given real numbers, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). The **damped driven oscillator model** with data $(m,c,k,f)$ is the second-order equation

$$m\,x''(t)+c\,x'(t)+k\,x(t)=f(t),\qquad t\in I .$$

A **solution** of the model on an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior is a twice differentiable $x:J\to\mathbb R$ such that the identity holds for every $t\in J$, derivatives being ordinary real derivatives ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The model is called **homogeneous** when $f\equiv 0$, **undamped** when $c=0$, and **strictly damped** when $c>0$.

The **phase-plane equation** of the model has right-hand side

$$G_f:I\times\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad G_f(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{f(t)-c\,v-k\,x}{m}\Bigr).$$

Here $\mathbb R^2$ is the **phase plane**, with coordinates $(x,v)$, where $x$ is the **displacement** and $v$ the **velocity**. For an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior, a differentiable curve $z=(x,v):J\to\mathbb R^2$ solves the phase-plane equation when $z'(t)=G_f(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$, using the domain-relative derivative at any included endpoint ([[def-derivative]]). If $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$, then $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ solves this equation; conversely, if $t\mapsto(x(t),v(t))$ solves it, then $v=x'$ and $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$. When $J$ is open, this is the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] on the open domain $J\times\mathbb R^2$. For the homogeneous model the right-hand side is written $G_0(x,v)=(v,-(cv+kx)/m)$.

The **characteristic polynomial** of the model is

$$p(\lambda):=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k,$$

with **discriminant** $\Delta:=c^2-4mk$. When $k>0$ define the **undamped frequency** $\omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}$, the **damping rate** $\gamma:=c/(2m)$ and, when $4mk>c^2$, the **damped frequency** $\omega:=\sqrt{k/m-\gamma^2}=\sqrt{4mk-c^2}/(2m)$; the corresponding square roots are the nonnegative real ones.

Use the fixed coordinate, time and energy units and numerical matrix convention of [[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]]. Every displayed matrix identity and phase norm is in those numerical coordinates; physical positions, velocities, modal amplitudes, frequencies and energies are recovered by the stated fixed scale factors. This does not change the set of physical motions.

For real $u$, define the hyperbolic functions by
$\cosh u:=(e^{u}+e^{-u})/2$ and $\sinh u:=(e^{u}-e^{-u})/2$.

Global-time, growth and boundedness claims below refer to the unique maximal extension of the autonomous free equation on $\mathbb R$; local motions remain its restrictions. Values at $0$ in coefficient formulas are evaluated on that extension when the original interval omits $0$.

Adopt the free coupled quadratic model of
[[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]] with data $(M,K,J)$ in which
$J\equiv0$, $M$ is symmetric positive definite and $K$ is symmetric, with
modal data $M^{1/2}$, $M^{-1/2}$, $O$, $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n})$,
modal coordinates $z=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ and mode frequencies
$\omega_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}$ for $\lambda_{i}>0$. Write
$\kappa_{i}:=\sqrt{-\lambda_{i}}$ for $\lambda_{i}<0$. Then:

1. **Existence and uniqueness on the whole line.** For every $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$
and every datum $(q_{0},v_{0})\in\mathbb R^{2n}$ there is exactly one motion
$q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{n}$ with $q(t_{0})=q_{0}$ and $q'(t_{0})=v_{0}$; it
is the unique maximal motion through that datum.
2. **Complete modal classification.** A curve $q:J\to\mathbb R^{n}$ of class
$C^{2}$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a
motion of the free model if and only if its modal coordinates satisfy

$$z_{i}(t)=a_{i}\cos(\omega_{i}t)+b_{i}\sin(\omega_{i}t)\ (\lambda_{i}>0),\qquad z_{i}(t)=a_{i}+b_{i}t\ (\lambda_{i}=0),\qquad z_{i}(t)=a_{i}\cosh(\kappa_{i}t)+b_{i}\sinh(\kappa_{i}t)\ (\lambda_{i}<0)$$

for real numbers $a_{i},b_{i}$; the coefficients are unique and are
determined by the datum of the unique maximal extension through $a_{i}=z_{i}(0)$, $b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)/\omega_{i}$
for $\lambda_{i}>0$, $b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)$ for $\lambda_{i}=0$ and
$b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)/\kappa_{i}$ for $\lambda_{i}<0$.
3. **Energy and mode energies.** Along every motion the mechanical energy is
constant, and with $E_{i}:=\tfrac12\bigl(z_{i}'^{2}+\lambda_{i}z_{i}^{2}\bigr)$
one has $E(q,q')=\sum_{i=1}^{n}E_{i}$ and every $E_{i}$ is constant; for the
families of clause 2,

$$E_{i}=\tfrac12\omega_{i}^{2}\bigl(a_{i}^{2}+b_{i}^{2}\bigr)\ (\lambda_{i}>0),\qquad E_{i}=\tfrac12b_{i}^{2}\ (\lambda_{i}=0),\qquad E_{i}=\tfrac12\kappa_{i}^{2}\bigl(b_{i}^{2}-a_{i}^{2}\bigr)\ (\lambda_{i}<0).$$

4. **Degenerate families are intrinsic.** Let $\lambda$ be a modal stiffness,
let $E_{\lambda}^{S}:=\{u\in\mathbb R^{n}:M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}u=\lambda u\}$ and
let $N_{\lambda}:=M^{-1/2}E_{\lambda}^{S}$, a subspace of dimension equal to
the multiplicity of $\lambda$. A motion $q$ satisfies $z_{i}\equiv0$ for every
index $i$ with $\lambda_{i}\ne\lambda$ if and only if $q$ is a $C^{2}$ curve
with $q(t)\in N_{\lambda}$ for all $t$ in its interval and $q''+\lambda q=0$.
Consequently the family of such **pure-$\lambda$ motions** is independent of
the choice of diagonalization $O$: for $\lambda>0$ it consists exactly of
$q(t)=\cos(\omega t)q_{0}+\omega^{-1}\sin(\omega t)q_{1}$ with
$q_{0},q_{1}\in N_{\lambda}$ and $\omega=\sqrt{\lambda}$, for $\lambda=0$ of
$q(t)=q_{0}+tq_{1}$ with $q_{0},q_{1}\in N_{\lambda}$, and for $\lambda<0$ of
$q(t)=\cosh(\kappa t)q_{0}+\kappa^{-1}\sinh(\kappa t)q_{1}$ with
$\kappa=\sqrt{-\lambda}$. These formulas on a local interval are restrictions of their unique maximal extensions; $q_0,q_1$ are the position and velocity of that extension at time $0$, even if the local interval omits $0$. The individual modal vectors $u_{i}$ are not
intrinsic when the multiplicity exceeds one.
5. **Boundedness.** If $K$ is positive definite then every motion is bounded
on $\mathbb R$. If $K$ is non-negative and some $\lambda_{i}=0$, then a
motion with $z_{i}'\equiv b_{i}\ne0$ on a zero mode is unbounded on
$[0,\infty)$: the zero mode is affine, not oscillatory.
6. **Unstable direction.** If $K$ is not non-negative, then $(0,0)$ is not a
Lyapunov stable rest point of the free model
([[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]): there is $\varepsilon_{0}>0$
such that for every $\delta>0$ there are data with
$\lVert(q_{0},v_{0})\rVert_{2}<\delta$ whose motion reaches
$\lVert(q(t),q'(t))\rVert_{2}=\varepsilon_{0}$ at some time $t>0$.

The statement is read for the declared model data; no value of any parameter,
no physical realization and no measured frequency is asserted.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

derivations.claim: Clause 1 is the instantiation of [F1] at the data of the statement: the hypotheses are $M$ symmetric positive definite, $K$ symmetric non-negative, $I_{0}$ an interval with nonempty interior and $\varphi=J$ continuous, so the unique motion with the datum is $q=M^{-1/2}Oz$ with the displayed scalar solutions and $\psi=O^{\mathsf T}M^{-1/2}J$.
Sinusoidal modal force: for $J(t)=J_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$ linearity of the map $J\mapsto O^{\mathsf T}M^{-1/2}J$ gives $\psi(t)=O^{\mathsf T}M^{-1/2}J_{0}\cos(\Omega t)=\psi_{0}\cos(\Omega t)$.

Scalar particular solutions: for $\lambda_{i}>0$ and $\Omega^{2}\ne\lambda_{i}$, [F2] applies with $k=\lambda_{i}$ and $f_{0}=\psi_{0,i}$ and supplies the solution $\psi_{0,i}\cos(\Omega t)/(\lambda_{i}-\Omega^{2})$ of amplitude $|\psi_{0,i}|/|\lambda_{i}-\Omega^{2}|$, which is (a); for $\lambda_{i}>0$ and $\Omega^{2}=\lambda_{i}$, [F2] supplies $\psi_{0,i}t\sin(\omega_{i}t)/(2\omega_{i})$ and its unboundedness, which is (b); for $\lambda_{i}=0$ direct differentiation by [F5] gives $(-\psi_{0,i}\cos(\Omega t)/\Omega^{2})''=\psi_{0,i}\cos(\Omega t)$ when $\Omega>0$ and $(\psi_{0,i}t^{2}/2)''=\psi_{0,i}$ when $\Omega=0$, with the stated boundedness and unboundedness; this is (c).

Reduction: let $q$ be a motion of the forced model; the particular functions of step 2.1 for all indices combine into $z^{\mathrm{p}}$ with $z_{i}^{\mathrm{p}}$ solving $z_{i}''+\lambda_{i}z_{i}=\psi_{i}$, and $q^{\mathrm{p}}:=M^{-1/2}Oz^{\mathrm{p}}$ is a motion by [F1]; since the system $Mq''+Kq=J$ is linear, the difference $q^{\mathrm{h}}:=q-q^{\mathrm{p}}$ solves the free system $Mq''+Kq=0$, hence is a free motion, and by [F4] its modal coordinates are the oscillatory or affine families of [[pthm-cm09-free-modes-and-degeneracy]] clause 2.

Resonance: suppose some index $i$ has $\psi_{0,i}\ne0$ and is resonant in the sense of clause 3(a). If $\lambda_{i}>0$ and $\Omega^{2}=\lambda_{i}$, then the $i$-th modal coordinate of every motion is, by steps 3.1 and 1.1, the sum of the unbounded particular function $\psi_{0,i}t\sin(\omega_{i}t)/(2\omega_{i})$ of step 2.1(b) and a bounded homogeneous oscillatory function, hence is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$; if $\lambda_{i}=0$ and $\Omega=0$, it is the sum of the quadratic particular function $\psi_{0,i}t^{2}/2$ and an affine homogeneous function, hence also unbounded. Since the bijection $z\mapsto q=M^{-1/2}Oz$ with fixed coefficients preserves unboundedness by [F5], every motion of the model is unbounded; this is clause 3(a).

Boundedness: suppose $K$ is positive definite, so every $\lambda_{i}>0$ by [[pthm-cm09-free-modes-and-degeneracy]] clause 5, and no index with $\psi_{0,i}\ne0$ has $\Omega^{2}=\lambda_{i}$. For every nonresonant index use the bounded particular function of step 2.1(a); if $\Omega^2=\lambda_i$, the hypothesis gives $\psi_{0,i}=0$ and the particular function of step 2.1(b) is identically zero and the homogeneous functions of step 3.1 are bounded oscillations by [F4]; hence every modal coordinate and its derivative are bounded on $[0,\infty)$, and by the fixed-coefficient bijection of [F5] every motion $(q,q')$ is bounded; this is clause 3(b). The list of resonant frequencies in clause 3 is the direct reading of the cases of step 2.1.

Clauses 1-3 are proved. The generalized force is prescribed external data in the modelling status of [F3]: the model has no back-reaction, no damping, and the resonance statement is a property of the declared undamped forced model, not a measured response.
