citations.quote:
**(i) Setting.** Work in the one-dimensional model class of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]] with time window
$I_{0}=\mathbb R$, configuration domain $Q=\mathbb R$, a fixed mass $m>0$,
the spring constant $k>0$ of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]], and a **drag
coefficient** $c\ge0$ of dimension $\mu\tau^{-1}$, read in kilograms per
second ([[def-cm01-units]]). The model's force law is declared through the
additive composition of force contributions, in the sense of clause (v) of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]], read in one coordinate:
$$F(x,v)=-k\,x-c\,v .$$

The **damped oscillator model** is the one-dimensional model with this force
law; its equation of motion is
$$m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0,$$
and its data $(m,c,k,0)$ are oscillator-type data in the sense of clause (f)
of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]. The model is
autonomous and depends on the velocity; it is **undamped** when $c=0$, in
which case it is exactly the harmonic model of [[post-cm04-harmonic-model]],
and **strictly damped** when $c>0$.

**(ii) Potential presentation with a residual force.** The model presents its
force law through the harmonic potential $U(x)=\tfrac12kx^{2}$ of
[[post-cm04-harmonic-model]] together with the **residual force**
$$d(t,x,v)=-c\,v,$$
in the sense of clause (d) of [[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]]:
$F(x,v)=-U'(x)+d(t,x,v)$. The mechanical energy of the model is therefore
the function $E(x,v)=\tfrac12mv^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}$ of clause (d), defined
along every motion; the drag force is not presented through a potential and
the model is not a global potential model when $c>0$.

**(iii) Regularity.** Let
$X:=x_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm m)$ and
$V:=v_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{m/s})$ be the dimensionless numerical SI state
coordinates (the real state coordinates in the displayed force-map signature),
and let $K:=k_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{N/m})$,
$C:=c_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm{kg/s})$ be the numerical coefficients. The
numerical force map $\widehat F:=F_{\rm phys}/(1\,\mathrm N)$ is
$\widehat F(X,V)=-KX-CV$, so
$$\lvert\widehat F(X,V)-\widehat F(X',V')\rvert\le K\lvert X-X'\rvert+C\lvert V-V'\rvert\le(K+C)\,\lVert(X,V)-(X',V')\rVert_{2}.$$
The real number $K+C$ is a Lipschitz constant for this normalized numerical
coordinate map; the dimensionful coefficients $k$ and $c$ are not added.
The force map is continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable,
uniformly in time ([[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]). It is an
admissible force law of the class of clause (a) of
[[def-cm04-one-dimensional-models-and-equilibria]], and its equation is
exactly the homogeneous model $m\,x''+cx'+kx=0$ of
[[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]].

**(iv) Physical status and regime.** The drag term is a **phenomenological**
constitutive model, adopted rather than derived: it represents the net force
of a medium whose microscopic state is not part of the model. The linear
velocity-proportional form is a restricted regime — slow motion through a
viscous medium, of which the Stokes force $c=6\pi\eta a$ is the recorded
example in the framework's drag postulate [[post-cm02-drag]] — and the
coefficient $c$ is a model parameter depending on body and medium. Other
regimes are different models: drag growing quadratically with speed, or
Coulomb sliding friction, whose force contains the factor $v/\lvert v\rvert$
and is undefined at $v=0$ and is not of the standing regularity. The model
also neglects the random component of the environment's force; the recorded
source states that this neglect is admissible only in a stated energy regime,
in which the oscillator's energy greatly exceeds the energy scale of the
environment's fluctuations. No value of $c$, $m$ or $k$ is asserted, and a
measured value used in an application is an empirical premise with its own
conditions and uncertainty.

**(v) Status.** Adopted assumption of the framework when a model invokes it;
the damped oscillator selects no law of nature on its own, and no
fluctuation–dissipation relation is asserted. Its conditional consequences
are the subject of the damped-motion theorems of this page.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k\in\mathbb R$ be given real numbers, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). The **damped driven oscillator model** with data $(m,c,k,f)$ is the second-order equation

$$m\,x''(t)+c\,x'(t)+k\,x(t)=f(t),\qquad t\in I .$$

A **solution** of the model on an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior is a twice differentiable $x:J\to\mathbb R$ such that the identity holds for every $t\in J$, derivatives being ordinary real derivatives ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The model is called **homogeneous** when $f\equiv 0$, **undamped** when $c=0$, and **strictly damped** when $c>0$.

The **phase-plane equation** of the model has right-hand side

$$G_f:I\times\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad G_f(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{f(t)-c\,v-k\,x}{m}\Bigr).$$

Here $\mathbb R^2$ is the **phase plane**, with coordinates $(x,v)$, where $x$ is the **displacement** and $v$ the **velocity**. For an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior, a differentiable curve $z=(x,v):J\to\mathbb R^2$ solves the phase-plane equation when $z'(t)=G_f(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$, using the domain-relative derivative at any included endpoint ([[def-derivative]]). If $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$, then $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ solves this equation; conversely, if $t\mapsto(x(t),v(t))$ solves it, then $v=x'$ and $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$. When $J$ is open, this is the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] on the open domain $J\times\mathbb R^2$. For the homogeneous model the right-hand side is written $G_0(x,v)=(v,-(cv+kx)/m)$.

The **characteristic polynomial** of the model is

$$p(\lambda):=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k,$$

with **discriminant** $\Delta:=c^2-4mk$. When $k>0$ define the **undamped frequency** $\omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}$, the **damping rate** $\gamma:=c/(2m)$ and, when $4mk>c^2$, the **damped frequency** $\omega:=\sqrt{k/m-\gamma^2}=\sqrt{4mk-c^2}/(2m)$; the corresponding square roots are the nonnegative real ones.

Let $n\ge1$, equip $\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], let $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), let $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and $z_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The Euclidean norm is a norm by [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], and the standard coordinate vectors form an ordered basis by [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]. For $A=(a_{ij})$ and $z\in\mathbb R^n$, define $(Az)_i:=\sum_{j<n}a_{ij}z_j$; this is a linear map by [[def-linear-map]], hence bounded by [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]], and $\|A\|$ denotes its induced Euclidean operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Matrix powers and products use [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]; their action agrees with composition of the corresponding linear maps by distributing the finite sums in the displayed coordinate formula. Define the **matrix exponential**

$$E:\mathbb R\longrightarrow M_n(\mathbb R),\qquad E(t):=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{t^k}{k!}A^k .$$

Then:

1. $E$ is well defined and of class $C^1$, with $E(0)=I_n$, $E(u+v)=E(u)E(v)$, $\frac{d}{du}E(u)=AE(u)=E(u)A$ for all $u,v\in\mathbb R$, and $\|E(u)\|\le e^{\|A\||u|}$ for the operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]) subordinate to the Euclidean norm.
2. The map
$$z:\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n,\qquad z(t):=E(t-t_0)z_0+\int_{t_0}^tE(t-s)b(s)\,ds,$$
satisfies $z(t_0)=z_0$ and $z'(t)=A\,z(t)+b(t)$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$.
3. Uniqueness: if $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval with nonempty interior containing $t_0$ ([[def-interval]]) and $w:J\to\mathbb R^n$ is differentiable with $w'=Aw+b$ on $J$ and $w(t_0)=z_0$, then $w=z|_J$.

Let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ and $y:J\to\mathbb R^n$ solve the same IVP. The solution $y$ is an **extension** of $x$ when $I\subseteq J$ and $y|_I=x$. It is a proper extension when $I\subsetneq J$.

A solution is **maximal** when it has no proper extension. Its domain is its **maximal interval of existence**. A solution is **global** when its domain is the entire time projection allowed by the ODE domain; for a vector field on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$, this means domain $\mathbb R$.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Call $G : I \to \mathbb{R}$ a **primitive of $f$ on
$I$** when $G$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ as a function on $I$ with
$G' = f$ there ([[def-derivative]]). Then:

1. **Existence.** Fix $c_0 \in I$. The function
   $$F : I \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad F(x) \;:=\; \int_{c_0}^x f$$
   is defined at every $x \in I$ ([[def-oriented-integral]],
   [[def-the-integral-function]]) and is a primitive of $f$ on $I$.
2. **Uniqueness up to a constant.** If $G_1$ and $G_2$ are primitives of $f$ on
   $I$ then there is a real $k$ with $G_1(x) = G_2(x) + k$ for every $x \in I$.
3. **Evaluation.** If $a, b \in I$ with $a < b$ and $G$ is any primitive of $f$
   on $I$, then
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**The scope is exactly the continuous case, and that is not a limitation of the
proof.** An integrable function need not have a primitive, and a function with a
primitive need not be integrable; this corollary is precisely the intersection
where both fundamental theorems apply, and both witnesses are on the companion
page.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $n\ge1$, $P>0$, let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, continuously partially differentiable in the second variable and $P$-periodic in time, with average $\bar f$ and deviation $g$ as in [[def-cm-averaging-data-and-averaged-field]]. Here $D_xf(t,x)$ is the total derivative in the state variable defined in [[lem-cm-averaging-data-basic-bounds]]. Let $x_0\in O$, let $0<\rho<R$ with $\overline B(x_0,R)\subseteq O$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), and let $M,L\ge0$ satisfy

$$\|f(t,x)\|_2\le M,\qquad \|D_xf(t,x)\|\le L\qquad\bigl(t\in\mathbb R,\ x\in\overline B(x_0,R)\bigr),$$

$\|\cdot\|$ being the operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Put

$$B:=2MP,\qquad B_1:=2LP,\qquad K:=e^{LA}\bigl[B+(LB+B_1M)A\bigr],$$

where $\varepsilon>0$ and $A>0$ are parameters. Suppose $y:[0,A/\varepsilon]\to\overline B(x_0,R-\rho)$ is a solution of the averaged system

$$y'(t)=\varepsilon\bar f(y(t)),\qquad y(0)=x_0 .$$

If $\varepsilon K<\rho$, then the solution $x$ of $x'(t)=\varepsilon f(t,x(t))$, $x(0)=x_0$ exists on all of $[0,A/\varepsilon]$ and satisfies, for every $t\in[0,A/\varepsilon]$,

$$\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2\le\varepsilon K=\varepsilon\,e^{LA}\bigl[B+(LB+B_1M)A\bigr].$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $P>0$, let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]). Assume that for each standard coordinate vector $e_j$ of $\mathbb R^n$, $0\le j<n$, and every $(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times O$, the vector-valued derivative at $r=0$ of $r\mapsto f(t,x+r e_j)$ exists, and that each resulting partial derivative $(t,x)\mapsto\partial_{x_j}f(t,x)$ is continuous on $\mathbb R\times O$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). This is the meaning of **continuously partially differentiable in the state variable** here. Suppose also that $f$ is **$P$-periodic in time**, that is

$$f(t+P,x)=f(t,x)\qquad\text{for all }(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times O .$$

The **average** of such an $f$ is the map

$$\bar f:O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n,\qquad \bar f(x):=\frac1P\int_0^Pf(s,x)\,ds,$$

where the integral is the componentwise Riemann integral of the continuous curve $s\mapsto f(s,x)$ over the compact interval $[0,P]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]); it is well defined and finite for every $x\in O$ because that curve is continuous. The **oscillatory part** of $f$ is $f-\bar f$, and the **deviation** of $f$ is

$$g:[0,P]\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n,\qquad g(t,x):=\int_0^t\bigl(f(s,x)-\bar f(x)\bigr)\,ds .$$

Because $\int_0^Pf(s,x)-\bar f(x)\,ds=P\bar f(x)-P\bar f(x)=0$ by linearity and additivity of the integral ([[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]]), the formula $g(t+kP,x):=g(t,x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$ and $t\in[0,P)$ defines a unique extension, again written $g$, to all of $\mathbb R\times O$; it satisfies $g(t+P,x)=g(t,x)$ and $g(0,x)=0$ for all $(t,x)$, and on $[0,P]$ it is the integral displayed above.

The **averaged (or reduced) system** of $f$ for a parameter $\varepsilon>0$ is the autonomous first-order system on $O$

$$y'(t)=\varepsilon\,\bar f(y(t)).$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $x \in X$ and let
$r \in \mathbb{R}$ with $r > 0$ ([[def-real-order]]). Define

$$B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) < r \,\}, \qquad \bar B(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) \le r \,\}, \qquad S(x,r) := \{\, y \in X : d(x,y) = r \,\}.$$

$B(x,r)$ is the **open ball**, $\bar B(x,r)$ the **closed ball** and $S(x,r)$ the
**sphere** of **centre** $x$ and **radius** $r$. The radius is always a strictly
positive real; a ball of radius $0$ or of negative radius is never written in
this library.

**Immediate consequences of the definitions.** For every $x \in X$ and $r > 0$:

- $x \in B(x,r)$, because $d(x,x) = 0 < r$ (axiom (M1) of [[def-metric-space]]);
  in particular open and closed balls are nonempty.
- $B(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, and
  $\bar B(x,r)$ is the disjoint union of $B(x,r)$ and $S(x,r)$, by trichotomy of
  the order of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]):
  each $y$ satisfies exactly one of $d(x,y) < r$, $d(x,y) = r$, $d(x,y) > r$.
- If $0 < s \le r$ then $B(x,s) \subseteq B(x,r)$ and
  $\bar B(x,s) \subseteq \bar B(x,r)$, by transitivity of the order.
- Nonnegativity of the metric ([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]) is what forces the
  radius convention, and it forces it for the **open** ball only: if $r \le 0$
  then $B(x,r) = \{y : d(x,y) < r\}$ is empty, because $d(x,y) \ge 0 \ge r$
  for every $y$. The other two sets behave differently at $r = 0$, and the
  convention $r > 0$ excludes them for uniformity rather than for emptiness:
  $\bar B(x,0) = S(x,0) = \{x\}$, since $d(x,y) \le 0$ together with
  $d(x,y) \ge 0$ gives $d(x,y) = 0$ and hence $y = x$ by (M1). For $r < 0$ all
  three sets are empty.

**A sphere may be empty, and so the three sets are not on a par.** For $r > 0$
the open and closed balls always contain $x$, but nothing in the definition
produces a point at distance exactly $r$ from $x$. If a metric takes only the
values $0$ and $1$, as the discrete metric on the companion page does, then
$S(x,2) = \emptyset$ while $B(x,2) = \bar B(x,2)$ is the whole space. So
nonemptiness of a sphere is never available by convention: where it is used, it
is proved.

**The ambient space is part of the notation.** $B(x,r)$ depends on $(X,d)$ and
not on $x$ and $r$ alone. When more than one space or more than one metric is in
play we write $B_X(x,r)$, or $B_d(x,r)$, and likewise for $\bar B$ and $S$. This
matters as soon as subspaces appear ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]): a
ball of a subspace is the trace on it of a ball of the ambient space, and the two
are different sets.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ carries the
Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
[[def-p-norms-on-rn]], whose induced metric is the published $d_2$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]],
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). A function into $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is called
**vector-valued**.

### Continuity

Let $(X, d_X)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$
carry the restricted metric $d_A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]), let
$f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $a \in A$. Then $f$ is **continuous at $a$**
when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ d_X(x,a) < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ \lVert f(x) - f(a)\rVert_2 < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon, \delta$ ranging over the positive reals, and **continuous on
$A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**This is not a new notion, and that is the point of writing it down.** Since
$\lVert f(x)-f(a)\rVert_2 = d_2\bigl(f(x),f(a)\bigr)$ and $d_A$ is the
restriction of $d_X$, the displayed condition is **verbatim** the condition of
[[def-metric-continuity]] for the map of metric spaces
$f : (A,d_A) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$. So every theorem about continuous maps
of metric spaces applies to vector-valued functions with no translation, and
this library has exactly one notion of continuity here. The same move was made
once before, between the $\mathbb{R}$-native and the metric notions, in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]]; this item is that move one dimension up in
the codomain.

The two cases used below are $X = \mathbb{R}$ with $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) and $X = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $d_2$, for
$n \ge 1$.

### Limits, for a real domain

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$, let $c$ be a limit
point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. We say
$f(x)$ **tends to $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$**, and write
$\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$, when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ 0 < |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ \lVert f(x) - L\rVert_2 < \varepsilon\ \bigr].$$

This is the condition of [[def-function-limit]] with the absolute value in the
codomain replaced by $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$; as there, the puncture $0 < |x-c|$ is
what makes $c$ a point the function need not be defined at, and the hypothesis
that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is what stops the condition from being satisfied
vacuously.

**The notation denotes: at most one $L$ satisfies the condition.** Suppose $L$
and $L'$ both do and $L \ne L'$. Then $\varepsilon := \lVert L-L'\rVert_2 / 2 > 0$
by (N1) for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). Take $\delta$
and $\delta'$ for this $\varepsilon$ and put $\eta := \min\{\delta,\delta'\} > 0$.
Since $c$ is a limit point of $A$ there is $x \in A$ with $0 < |x-c| < \eta$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), and then

$$\lVert L - L'\rVert_2 \;\le\; \lVert L - f(x)\rVert_2 + \lVert f(x) - L'\rVert_2 \;<\; \varepsilon + \varepsilon \;=\; \lVert L-L'\rVert_2$$

by (N3) and (N2), which trichotomy forbids. So $L = L'$.

### Components

For $i < m$ define the $i$-th **coordinate projection**
$\pi_i : \mathbb{R}^{m} \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\pi_i(y) := y_i = y(i)$, and for
$f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ the $i$-th **component** $f_i := \pi_i \circ f$, a
real-valued function on $A$.

**Each $\pi_i$ is $1$-Lipschitz** ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]): for
$y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$,

$$\bigl|\pi_i(y) - \pi_i(z)\bigr| \;=\; |y_i - z_i| \;\le\; \lVert y - z\rVert_2 \;=\; d_2(y,z),$$

the middle inequality being $|w_i| \le \lVert w\rVert_2$ at $w := y-z$
([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] clause 3, or
directly because $w_i^{2}$ is one term of the sum $\sum_{k<m}w_k^{2}$). Written
in coordinates, $f(x)$ is the vector whose $i$-th coordinate is $f_i(x)$, and
$f(x) = \sum_{i<m} f_i(x)\,e_i$ in the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]).

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

derivations.claim: Identification of the slow system. Let $x$ be a motion and put $u(t):=\omega_{0}x(t)+ix'(t)$, so that $\zeta=e^{i\omega_{0}t}u/\sqrt{2\omega_{0}}$ and $\operatorname{Im}u=\sqrt{2\omega_{0}}\bigl(\cos(\omega_{0}t)\operatorname{Im}\zeta-\sin(\omega_{0}t)\operatorname{Re}\zeta\bigr)$ by [F2]. From $x''=-\omega_{0}^{2}x-(\varepsilon\gamma/m)x'$ of the model, $u'=\omega_{0}x'+ix''=\omega_{0}x'-i\omega_{0}^{2}x-i\frac{\varepsilon\gamma}{m}x'=-i\omega_{0}u-i\frac{\varepsilon\gamma}{m}\operatorname{Im}u,$ so differentiating $\zeta$ with the product and chain rules of [F2] gives $\zeta'=-\frac{i\varepsilon\gamma}{m}\frac{e^{i\omega_{0}t}}{\sqrt{2\omega_{0}}}\operatorname{Im}u=\varepsilon F(t,\zeta)$. Conversely, if $\zeta$ solves $\zeta'=\varepsilon F(t,\zeta)$ and $u:=\sqrt{2\omega_{0}}e^{-i\omega_{0}t}\zeta$, then $u'=-i\omega_{0}u-i(\varepsilon\gamma/m)\operatorname{Im}u$, so $x:=\operatorname{Re}(u)/\omega_{0}$ satisfies $x'=\operatorname{Re}(u')/\omega_{0}=\operatorname{Im}u$ and $x''=\operatorname{Im}(u')=-\omega_{0}\operatorname{Re}u-(\varepsilon\gamma/m)\operatorname{Im}u=-\omega_{0}^{2}x-(\varepsilon\gamma/m)x'$, that is, $x$ is a motion with the stated inverse formula. The two constructions are inverse to each other because $x$ and $x'$ are recovered from $\zeta$ and $\zeta$ is recovered from $x,x'$.

Smoothness, periodicity and average. $F$ is smooth on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb C$ because $\zeta\mapsto F(t,\zeta)$ is real-linear and the coefficients $t\mapsto e^{i\omega_{0}t}\cos(\omega_{0}t)$ and $t\mapsto e^{i\omega_{0}t}\sin(\omega_{0}t)$ are smooth; it is $P$-periodic with $P=2\pi/\omega_{0}$ because $e^{i\omega_{0}(t+P)}=e^{i\omega_{0}t}$ and $\cos(\omega_{0}(t+P))=\cos(\omega_{0}t)$, $\sin(\omega_{0}(t+P))=\sin(\omega_{0}t)$. Expanding the product, $F(t,\zeta)=\frac{\gamma}{m}\Bigl(\sin(\omega_{0}t)\cos(\omega_{0}t)\operatorname{Im}\zeta-\sin^{2}(\omega_{0}t)\operatorname{Re}\zeta\Bigr)-\frac{i\gamma}{m}\Bigl(\cos^{2}(\omega_{0}t)\operatorname{Im}\zeta-\sin(\omega_{0}t)\cos(\omega_{0}t)\operatorname{Re}\zeta\Bigr),$ so by [F3] the one-period average of the first bracket is $-\gamma\operatorname{Re}\zeta/(2m)$ and that of the second is $-\gamma\operatorname{Im}\zeta/(2m)$, giving $\bar F(\zeta)=-\frac{\gamma}{2m}(\operatorname{Re}\zeta+i\operatorname{Im}\zeta)=-\frac{\gamma}{2m}\zeta$. The averaged system is linear with constant coefficient and has the displayed global exponential solution. This is clause 2.

Bounds on the ball. For $\lvert\zeta-\zeta_{0}\rvert\le R$ one has $\lvert\zeta\rvert\le\lvert\zeta_{0}\rvert+R$, so $\lVert F(t,\zeta)\rVert_{2}=\frac{\gamma}{m}\bigl\lvert\cos(\omega_{0}t)\operatorname{Im}\zeta-\sin(\omega_{0}t)\operatorname{Re}\zeta\bigr\rvert\le\frac{\gamma}{m}\bigl(\lvert\operatorname{Im}\zeta\rvert+\lvert\operatorname{Re}\zeta\rvert\bigr)\le\frac{\gamma}{m}\sqrt2\,\bigl(\lvert\zeta_{0}\rvert+R\bigr)=M .$ The state derivative is $D_{\zeta}F(t,\zeta)h=-(i\gamma/m)e^{i\omega_{0}t}\bigl(\cos(\omega_{0}t)\operatorname{Im}h-\sin(\omega_{0}t)\operatorname{Re}h\bigr)$, whose modulus is at most $(\gamma/m)\sqrt2\,\lvert h\rvert$ by the same inequality, so $\lVert D_{\zeta}F(t,\zeta)\rVert\le L=(\gamma/m)\sqrt2$ by [F5].

Existence and uniqueness. By [F1] every datum has exactly one maximal motion and it is defined on all of $\mathbb R$; by step 1.1 its amplitude solves the slow system on $\mathbb R$ with the datum $\zeta(0)$, and distinct motions have distinct amplitudes. Conversely a solution of the slow system on $\mathbb R$ produces a motion by step 1.1; this proves the bijection of clause 1.

Averaged trajectory and the estimate. The averaged solution is $\bar\zeta(t)=\zeta_0e^{-\varepsilon\gamma t/(2m)}$, and its distance from $\zeta_0$ is $|\zeta_0|(1-e^{-\varepsilon\gamma t/(2m)})$. Thus the trajectory stays in the required ball exactly when the endpoint displacement is at most $R-\rho$; [F6] gives the equivalent logarithmic sufficient condition in clause 3. Apply the numerical rescaling specified in the Statement; write its numerical variables and constants without hats in this argument. The exact amplitude is already global by step 2.1. For $g(t,w):=\int_0^t(F(s,w)-\bar F(w))ds$, periodicity and the vanishing one-period integral give $g(0,w)=0$, $|g(t,w)|\le2MP=B$ and $\|D_wg(t,w)\|\le2LP=B_1$ on $|w-\zeta_0|\le R$: reduce $t$ modulo $P$ and integrate the bounds $2M$, $2L$ on the remaining interval. Smoothness of $F$ justifies differentiating this primitive in $w$. Before the first exit of the global exact amplitude from this ball, put $d=\zeta-\varepsilon g(t,\zeta)$ and $w=d-\bar\zeta$. The chain rule gives $w'=\varepsilon(\bar F(\zeta)-\bar F(\bar\zeta))-\varepsilon^2D_wg(t,\zeta)F(t,\zeta)$, with $w(0)=0$, hence $|w(t)|\le\int_0^t(\varepsilon L|w(s)|+\varepsilon^2(LB+B_1M))ds$. Put $a=\varepsilon L$ and $b=\varepsilon^2(LB+B_1M)$, and $r(t)=\int_0^t(a|w(s)|+b)ds$. Then $|w|\le r$, $r(0)=0$, $r'\le ar+b$ and $(e^{-at}r(t))'\le b e^{-at}$; integration gives $|w(t)|\le r(t)\le bt e^{at}=\varepsilon^2(LB+B_1M)t e^{\varepsilon Lt}$. Thus on $0\le t\le A/\varepsilon$ before any exit, $|\zeta-\bar\zeta|\le\varepsilon[B+(LB+B_1M)Ae^{LA}]\le\varepsilon K$. At a first exit time in this horizon, continuity would imply $R=|\zeta-\zeta_0|\le\varepsilon K+(R-\rho)<R$, a contradiction. There is no finite-existence-endpoint issue because the exact curve is global. The estimate therefore holds over the whole horizon; undoing the explicitly stated time/amplitude rescaling gives clause 3 with its physical units.

Energy identity and estimate. With $\zeta=(1/\sqrt{2\omega_{0}})(\omega_{0}x+ix')e^{i\omega_{0}t}$ one has $2\omega_{0}\lvert\zeta\rvert^{2}=\omega_{0}^{2}x^{2}+x'^{2}$ by [F2], hence $m\omega_{0}\lvert\zeta\rvert^{2}=\tfrac12 m x'^{2}+\tfrac12 m\omega_{0}^{2}x^{2}=\tfrac12mx'^{2}+\tfrac12kx^{2}=E .$ For $0\le t\le A/\varepsilon$, $\bigl\lvert\,\lvert\zeta(t)\rvert^{2}-\lvert\bar\zeta(t)\rvert^{2}\bigr\rvert=\bigl\lvert\lvert\zeta(t)\rvert-\lvert\bar\zeta(t)\rvert\bigr\rvert\bigl(\lvert\zeta(t)\rvert+\lvert\bar\zeta(t)\rvert\bigr)\le\varepsilon K\bigl(2\lvert\zeta_{0}\rvert+\varepsilon K\bigr)$, because $\lvert\zeta(t)\rvert\le\lvert\bar\zeta(t)\rvert+\varepsilon K\le\lvert\zeta_{0}\rvert+\varepsilon K$; multiplying by $m\omega_{0}$ and using $m\omega_{0}\lvert\bar\zeta(t)\rvert^{2}=E_{0}e^{-\varepsilon\gamma t/m}$ gives the displayed energy estimate; this is clause 4.

Clauses 1-4 are proved. The averaged equation defines a different model from the exact one; the estimate is finite-time, of order $\varepsilon$ in the amplitude, and holds only on the stated horizon under the smallness and trapping hypotheses; no exact decay law and no empirical qualification is asserted.

citations.quote:
**(a) Data of a coupled quadratic model.** A **coupled quadratic model** (a
**quadratic oscillator model**) is declared by the following data: an integer
$n\ge1$, the number of **degrees of freedom**; a **mass metric matrix**
$M\in M_{n}(\mathbb R)$, symmetric and positive definite, that is
$M=M^{\mathsf T}$ and $v^{\mathsf T}Mv>0$ for every nonzero
$v\in\mathbb R^{n}$ ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); a **stiffness matrix**
$K\in M_{n}(\mathbb R)$, symmetric, $K=K^{\mathsf T}$; and an interval $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior
([[def-interval]]) together with a continuous **generalized force**
$J:I_{0}\to\mathbb R^{n}$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]).
When no force or time interval is prescribed, take $I_0:=\mathbb R$ and
$J(t):=0$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$; in particular this is the convention
for the small-oscillation model in clause (d).
The coordinates $q_{1},\dots,q_{n}$ of $\mathbb R^{n}$ are read in the chart
in which the model is declared and carry declared dimensions
$\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{n}$ and units, and time is read in seconds and mass
in kilograms ([[def-cm01-units]]). The data carry the dimensions

$$[M_{ij}]=\mu\ell^{2}\gamma_{i}^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1},\qquad [K_{ij}]=\mu\ell^{2}\gamma_{i}^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1}\tau^{-2},\qquad [J_{i}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}\gamma_{i}^{-1},$$

so that $\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}Mv$, $\tfrac12q^{\mathsf T}Kq$ and the pairing
$J\cdot\delta q$ of the generalized force with a coordinate variation all have
the energy dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; if the coordinate $q_{i}$ is
length-valued, $\gamma_{i}=\ell$, the entry $J_{i}$ has the force dimension
$\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. This is the dimension bookkeeping of a generalized
coordinate description in the sense of
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]], whose kinetic metric and
generalized forces are the framework objects the data present; the matrices
$M$ and $K$ are model parameters, not measured quantities.

**Fixed-unit numerical convention.** Choose a positive coordinate unit $s_i$ of dimension $\gamma_i$ for each direction, a time unit $t_*>0$ and an energy unit $e_*>0$, held fixed throughout a model calculation. Matrix products, square roots, eigenvectors, derivatives and Euclidean norms below act on numerical coefficients in these units, not on arrays of unlike physical quantities. Explicitly, if $Q_i$, $\mathsf M_{ij}$, $\mathsf K_{ij}$ and $\mathsf J_i$ denote the dimensional data, the symbols in the algebra are
$$q_i=Q_i/s_i,\qquad t=t_{\mathrm{phys}}/t_*,\qquad M_{ij}=\mathsf M_{ij}s_is_j/(e_*t_*^2),\qquad K_{ij}=\mathsf K_{ij}s_is_j/e_*,\qquad J_i=\mathsf J_i s_i/e_*.$$
Then $Mq''+Kq=J$ is exactly the physical equation in these coefficients, $Q_i=s_iq_i$, $\dot Q_i=(s_i/t_*)q_i'$, and the physical energy is $e_*E$. This is an invertible choice of units, imposing no restriction on the dimensions $\gamma_i$. For a variable metric and potential the same convention means $U(q)=U_{\mathrm{phys}}(s_1q_1,\ldots,s_nq_n)/e_*$ and $M_{ij}(q)=\mathsf M_{ij}(s_1q_1,\ldots,s_nq_n)s_is_j/(e_*t_*^2)$. Congruence by the positive diagonal coordinate-scale matrix and multiplication by positive constants preserve symmetry, definiteness and critical-point type.

**(b) Model equation, motions and phase system.** On any interval with
nonempty interior, $C^r$ for $r=1,2$ means that the first $r$ derivatives
exist and are continuous on that interval, using the domain-relative
derivative of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] at included
endpoints; on open intervals this agrees with
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The equation of the model
with data $(M,K,J)$ is

$$M\,q''(t)+K\,q(t)=J(t)\qquad(t\in I_{0}).$$

A **motion** of the model is a curve $q:J\to\mathbb R^{n}$ of class $C^{2}$
on an interval
$J\subseteq I_{0}$ with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) satisfying the
equation for every $t\in J$. A **datum** at $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is a pair
$(q_{0},v_{0})\in\mathbb R^{n}\times\mathbb R^{n}$. The **phase system** of
the model is the first-order linear system $z'=A z+b(t)$ on
$I_{0}\times\mathbb R^{2n}$ with $z=(q,v)$ and

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_{n}\\-M^{-1}K&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad b(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\M^{-1}J(t)\end{pmatrix},$$

where $M^{-1}$ is the inverse of $M$. By the product rule and invertibility of
$M$, a $C^{1}$ curve $t\mapsto(q(t),v(t))$ solves the phase system if and only
if $q$ is a motion of the model and $v=q'$. The model is **free** when
$J\equiv0$ and **forced, with generalized force $J$,** otherwise; the read of
$J$ as a prescribed external generalized force is the modelling status of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] for the external contributions
of a force model.

**(c) Quadratic energies and the mass metric.** The **kinetic energy**, the
**potential energy of the stiffness** and the **mechanical energy** of the
model are

$$T(v):=\tfrac12\,v^{\mathsf T}Mv,\qquad U_{K}(q):=\tfrac12\,q^{\mathsf T}Kq,\qquad E(q,v):=T(v)+U_{K}(q),$$

whose physical readings are $e_*$ times the displayed numerical quantities, all of energy dimension. $U_{K}$ is defined for every symmetric $K$; the name
records that $K$ is the matrix through which the model enters, and when $K$ is
indefinite $U_{K}$ is not non-negative, the model is not presented by a
potential with a local minimum at the origin, and no stability vocabulary is
attached to it by this item. The quadratic form $v\mapsto v^{\mathsf T}Mv$ is
positive definite and is called the **mass metric** of the model; the word
"metric" records only this positive-definiteness, and no distance on
configuration space is defined here.

**(d) Small-oscillation model at an equilibrium.** Let a mechanical system in
a chart be given by a $C^{2}$ field $q\mapsto G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q)$ of
symmetric positive definite matrices on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb
R^{n}$ and a $C^{2}$ potential $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$
([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]), and let
$q_{0}\in\Omega$ be a **mechanical equilibrium**, $\nabla U(q_{0})=0$. Its
**small-oscillation model at $q_{0}$** is the coupled quadratic model with
degrees of freedom $n$, mass metric matrix $M:=G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q_{0})$,
**stiffness matrix** $K_{0}:=D^{2}U(q_{0})$ — the Hessian of the potential
([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], symmetric by
[[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]]) — and zero generalized force, read in the
displacement coordinates $\xi:=q-q_{0}$. When the chart arises from the
generalized-coordinate dictionary of
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]], the matrix
$G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q_{0})=DX(q_{0})^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q_{0})$ is the
value at $q_{0}$ of that dictionary's kinetic metric. This clause assigns
model data to the equilibrium; the identification of the assigned model with
the derivative of the mechanical field, and every statement about its motions,
are separate results and are not asserted here.

**(e) Modal vocabulary of the decoupling data.** All the following matrix operations use the fixed-unit numerical convention. By clauses 1-3 of [[lem-cm-positive-definite-matrix-square-roots]], $M^{1/2}$ and its inverse $M^{-1/2}$ exist and are symmetric positive definite. For every symmetric $K$, without a sign restriction, $S:=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}$ is symmetric, since $S^{\mathsf T}=M^{-1/2}K^{\mathsf T}M^{-1/2}=S$. The [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] therefore supplies an orthogonal $O$ and real diagonal $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$ with $S=O\Lambda O^{\mathsf T}$. This construction includes negative eigenvalues; the restricted non-negative-$K$ result [[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]] is used only in that restricted case. Define **modal coordinates** $z:=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ and **modal vectors** $u_i:=M^{-1/2}Oe_i$, the columns of the inverse transform $q=M^{-1/2}Oz$. The **modal stiffnesses** are the real numbers $\lambda_i$. Direct multiplication gives $Ku_i=\lambda_iMu_i$ and $u_i^{\mathsf T}Mu_j=\delta_{ij}$. In physical units put $a_*:=\sqrt{e_*}\,t_*$. A modal coordinate has unit $a_*$; the $j$-th component of a mass-normalized modal vector has unit $s_j/a_*$, and the physical coordinate is the sum of the physical modal-vector components times their modal amplitudes. The matrix entries of $O$ and its orthonormal eigenvectors are dimensionless numerical coefficients. The physical modal stiffness is $\lambda_i/t_*^2$; an oscillatory or hyperbolic coefficient has unit $a_*$, while the slope coefficient in a zero-mode family $a_i+b_it$ has unit $a_*/t_*$. The physical frequency is $\sqrt{\lambda_i}/t_*$ when $\lambda_i>0$.

An index is **oscillatory** when $\lambda_i>0$, with numerical frequency $\omega_i:=\sqrt{\lambda_i}$; it is a **zero mode** when $\lambda_i=0$, and an **unstable (exponential) direction** when $\lambda_i<0$. Distinct indices are **degenerate** when their stiffnesses agree. For real $\lambda$ define the **modal eigenspace** $E_\lambda:=\ker(K-\lambda M)$. Its dimension is the multiplicity of $\lambda$, because $q\mapsto M^{1/2}q$ bijects it with the $\lambda$-eigenspace of $S$. The model is **oscillatory** when $K$ is non-negative. Indeed $x^{\mathsf T}Sx=(M^{-1/2}x)^{\mathsf T}K(M^{-1/2}x)$, so $K\ge0$ exactly when every $\lambda_i\ge0$; positive definiteness likewise corresponds to all $\lambda_i>0$. The zero-mode multiplicity is $\dim\ker K$. Frequencies are read in radians per unit time under [[def-cm01-units]].

**(f) Status.** This item introduces objects, vocabulary, domains, regularity
and dimensions for the restricted model class of this page and assigns its
small-oscillation model to a mechanical equilibrium. It contains no
existence, uniqueness, conservation, stability, resonance, degeneracy or
approximation assertion; those are proved on this page as separate items. It
adopts no force law of nature and records no measured value. Every later
statement of this page names the data $(M,K,J)$ or the mechanical data
$(G_{\mathrm{kin}},U,q_{0})$ it uses, and the one-dimensional instance is
recorded in the remarks.

Use the fixed coordinate, time and energy units and numerical matrix convention of [[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]]. Every displayed matrix identity and phase norm is in those numerical coordinates; physical positions, velocities, modal amplitudes, frequencies and energies are recovered by the stated fixed scale factors. This does not change the set of physical motions.

For real $u$, define the hyperbolic functions by
$\cosh u:=(e^{u}+e^{-u})/2$ and $\sinh u:=(e^{u}-e^{-u})/2$.

Global-time, growth and boundedness claims below refer to the unique maximal extension of the autonomous free equation on $\mathbb R$; local motions remain its restrictions. Values at $0$ in coefficient formulas are evaluated on that extension when the original interval omits $0$.

Adopt the free coupled quadratic model of
[[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]] with data $(M,K,J)$ in which
$J\equiv0$, $M$ is symmetric positive definite and $K$ is symmetric, with
modal data $M^{1/2}$, $M^{-1/2}$, $O$, $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n})$,
modal coordinates $z=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ and mode frequencies
$\omega_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}$ for $\lambda_{i}>0$. Write
$\kappa_{i}:=\sqrt{-\lambda_{i}}$ for $\lambda_{i}<0$. Then:

1. **Existence and uniqueness on the whole line.** For every $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$
and every datum $(q_{0},v_{0})\in\mathbb R^{2n}$ there is exactly one motion
$q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{n}$ with $q(t_{0})=q_{0}$ and $q'(t_{0})=v_{0}$; it
is the unique maximal motion through that datum.
2. **Complete modal classification.** A curve $q:J\to\mathbb R^{n}$ of class
$C^{2}$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a
motion of the free model if and only if its modal coordinates satisfy

$$z_{i}(t)=a_{i}\cos(\omega_{i}t)+b_{i}\sin(\omega_{i}t)\ (\lambda_{i}>0),\qquad z_{i}(t)=a_{i}+b_{i}t\ (\lambda_{i}=0),\qquad z_{i}(t)=a_{i}\cosh(\kappa_{i}t)+b_{i}\sinh(\kappa_{i}t)\ (\lambda_{i}<0)$$

for real numbers $a_{i},b_{i}$; the coefficients are unique and are
determined by the datum of the unique maximal extension through $a_{i}=z_{i}(0)$, $b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)/\omega_{i}$
for $\lambda_{i}>0$, $b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)$ for $\lambda_{i}=0$ and
$b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)/\kappa_{i}$ for $\lambda_{i}<0$.
3. **Energy and mode energies.** Along every motion the mechanical energy is
constant, and with $E_{i}:=\tfrac12\bigl(z_{i}'^{2}+\lambda_{i}z_{i}^{2}\bigr)$
one has $E(q,q')=\sum_{i=1}^{n}E_{i}$ and every $E_{i}$ is constant; for the
families of clause 2,

$$E_{i}=\tfrac12\omega_{i}^{2}\bigl(a_{i}^{2}+b_{i}^{2}\bigr)\ (\lambda_{i}>0),\qquad E_{i}=\tfrac12b_{i}^{2}\ (\lambda_{i}=0),\qquad E_{i}=\tfrac12\kappa_{i}^{2}\bigl(b_{i}^{2}-a_{i}^{2}\bigr)\ (\lambda_{i}<0).$$

4. **Degenerate families are intrinsic.** Let $\lambda$ be a modal stiffness,
let $E_{\lambda}^{S}:=\{u\in\mathbb R^{n}:M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}u=\lambda u\}$ and
let $N_{\lambda}:=M^{-1/2}E_{\lambda}^{S}$, a subspace of dimension equal to
the multiplicity of $\lambda$. A motion $q$ satisfies $z_{i}\equiv0$ for every
index $i$ with $\lambda_{i}\ne\lambda$ if and only if $q$ is a $C^{2}$ curve
with $q(t)\in N_{\lambda}$ for all $t$ in its interval and $q''+\lambda q=0$.
Consequently the family of such **pure-$\lambda$ motions** is independent of
the choice of diagonalization $O$: for $\lambda>0$ it consists exactly of
$q(t)=\cos(\omega t)q_{0}+\omega^{-1}\sin(\omega t)q_{1}$ with
$q_{0},q_{1}\in N_{\lambda}$ and $\omega=\sqrt{\lambda}$, for $\lambda=0$ of
$q(t)=q_{0}+tq_{1}$ with $q_{0},q_{1}\in N_{\lambda}$, and for $\lambda<0$ of
$q(t)=\cosh(\kappa t)q_{0}+\kappa^{-1}\sinh(\kappa t)q_{1}$ with
$\kappa=\sqrt{-\lambda}$. These formulas on a local interval are restrictions of their unique maximal extensions; $q_0,q_1$ are the position and velocity of that extension at time $0$, even if the local interval omits $0$. The individual modal vectors $u_{i}$ are not
intrinsic when the multiplicity exceeds one.
5. **Boundedness.** If $K$ is positive definite then every motion is bounded
on $\mathbb R$. If $K$ is non-negative and some $\lambda_{i}=0$, then a
motion with $z_{i}'\equiv b_{i}\ne0$ on a zero mode is unbounded on
$[0,\infty)$: the zero mode is affine, not oscillatory.
6. **Unstable direction.** If $K$ is not non-negative, then $(0,0)$ is not a
Lyapunov stable rest point of the free model
([[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]): there is $\varepsilon_{0}>0$
such that for every $\delta>0$ there are data with
$\lVert(q_{0},v_{0})\rVert_{2}<\delta$ whose motion reaches
$\lVert(q(t),q'(t))\rVert_{2}=\varepsilon_{0}$ at some time $t>0$.

The statement is read for the declared model data; no value of any parameter,
no physical realization and no measured frequency is asserted.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k>0$, and consider the homogeneous damped oscillator model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0$ of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ identically zero, with characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k$, discriminant $\Delta=c^2-4mk$, damping rate $\gamma:=c/(2m)$, and, when applicable, roots
$$\lambda_\pm:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt\Delta}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \lambda:=-\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^2}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0).$$

A local solution here may have any interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. It has a unique extension to the global family below. A **maximal solution** means one that has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval; the maximal solutions of this global autonomous equation are precisely the family members on $\mathbb R$. For a homogeneous model restricted to a time domain $I$, its solutions have $J\subseteq I$ and are restrictions of these same global members; their extensions solve the all-$\mathbb R$ equation.

1. **Distinct real roots.** If $\Delta>0$, then $\lambda_+>\lambda_-$ are exactly the real roots of $p$, and a function $x:J\to\mathbb R$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a solution of the model if and only if
$$x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_+t}+Be^{\lambda_-t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

2. **Double real root.** If $\Delta=0$, then $\lambda=-c/(2m)$ is the only root of $p$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{\lambda t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

3. **Complex conjugate roots.** If $\Delta<0$, then $\omega>0$, the roots of $p$ are $-\gamma\pm i\omega$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)\bigr)\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

4. **Initial data.** In each of the three cases and for every $(x_0,v_0)\in\mathbb R^2$ there is exactly one solution $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$ and $x'(0)=v_0$. Its coefficients are
$$A=\frac{v_0-\lambda_-x_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-},\quad B=\frac{\lambda_+x_0-v_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}\quad(\Delta>0),\qquad A=x_0,\ B=v_0-\lambda x_0\quad(\Delta=0),$$
$$A=x_0,\quad B=\frac{v_0+\gamma x_0}{\omega}\quad(\Delta<0).$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

derivations.claim: Modal identities: $M$ is symmetric positive definite and $K$ is symmetric with $q^{\mathsf T}Kq=(k+c)(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2})-2cx_{1}x_{2}=k(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2})+c(x_{1}-x_{2})^{2}\ge0$ for $k>0, c>0$ (indeed positive definite), so the model is an oscillatory coupled quadratic model of [F1]. Multiplying, $Ku_{+}=(k,k)/\sqrt{2m}=k(1,1)/\sqrt{2m}=\frac{k}{m}Mu_{+}$ and $Ku_{-}=(k+2c,-(k+2c))/\sqrt{2m}=\frac{k+2c}{m}Mu_{-}$; and $u_{\pm}^{\mathsf T}Mu_{\pm}=m\lvert u_{\pm}\rvert_{2}^{2}=m\cdot\frac{2}{2m}=1$, $u_{+}^{\mathsf T}Mu_{-}=m(1-1)/(2m)=0$. This proves clause 1 with $\lambda_{\pm}$ as displayed.

Modal coordinates: with $e_{\pm}=(1,\pm1)/\sqrt2$ the matrix $O=[e_{+}\ e_{-}]$ is orthogonal and $M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}=\frac1mK$ has the orthonormal eigenbasis $e_{\pm}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_{\pm}$ by clause 1; hence $z=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ has $z_{\pm}=e_{\pm}^{\mathsf T}\sqrt m\,q=\sqrt{m/2}(x_{1}\pm x_{2})$ and $u_{\pm}=M^{-1/2}e_{\pm}$, so the modal data of clause (e) of [[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]] are exactly those displayed.

Frequency comparison: $\omega_{+}=\sqrt{k/m}$ contains no $c$, while $c\mapsto\omega_{-}=\sqrt{(k+2c)/m}$ is strictly increasing on $c>0$ with $\omega_{-}>\omega_{+}$: the in-phase oscillation is softer than the anti-phase one. This is clause 4.

Zero stiffness: if $k=0$ then $K=c\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $Ku_{+}=0$ and $Ku_{-}=\frac{2c}{m}Mu_{-}$, so $\lambda_{+}=0$ and $\lambda_{-}=2c/m$; by [F2] the general motion is the affine-plus-oscillatory family displayed in clause 5, in which the pair translates as a whole (arbitrary constant velocity $B$) and only the relative coordinate $x_{1}-x_{2}$ oscillates, with $\omega_{-}=\sqrt{2c/m}$. This is clause 5.

Motions: by [F2] and [F4], every motion is the superposition of clause 2 with $\lambda_{\pm}>0$, i.e. the displayed two-frequency family, and the coefficients $(A,B,C,D)$ are bijective onto the data $(q(0),q'(0))=\bigl(Au_{+}+Cu_{-},\,B\omega_{+}u_{+}+D\omega_{-}u_{-}\bigr)$. This is clause 2.

Single-mode data: for $q(0)=u_{+}$, $q'(0)=0$ the coefficient system gives $A=1$, $B=C=D=0$, so $q(t)=\cos(\omega_{+}t)u_{+}$; its energy is $E=\tfrac12q'^{\mathsf T}Mq'+\tfrac12q^{\mathsf T}Kq =\tfrac12\omega_{+}^{2}\sin^{2}(\omega_{+}t)+\tfrac12\tfrac{k}{m}\cos^{2}(\omega_{+}t)=\tfrac{k}{2m}$, constant because $\omega_{+}^{2}=k/m$; the same computation with $\lambda_{-}=(k+2c)/m$ gives $E=(k+2c)/(2m)$ for the anti-phase datum. This is clause 3.
Clauses 1-5 are verified on the explicit data; all parameters are model data with declared units, and no measured frequency, damping or apparatus behaviour is asserted.
