Multiplied both eigenpairs and M norms: squared norms 2ml^2(2±sqrt2), mixed product zero. Two distinct positive eigenvalues give complete bounded global modes and pure-mode initial data. Matrices are explicitly attributed small-oscillation data; no derivation from full nonlinear rods claimed. Radian fixed-unit coefficients and modal amplitude units consistent.

citations.quote:
**(a) Data of a coupled quadratic model.** A **coupled quadratic model** (a
**quadratic oscillator model**) is declared by the following data: an integer
$n\ge1$, the number of **degrees of freedom**; a **mass metric matrix**
$M\in M_{n}(\mathbb R)$, symmetric and positive definite, that is
$M=M^{\mathsf T}$ and $v^{\mathsf T}Mv>0$ for every nonzero
$v\in\mathbb R^{n}$ ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); a **stiffness matrix**
$K\in M_{n}(\mathbb R)$, symmetric, $K=K^{\mathsf T}$; and an interval $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior
([[def-interval]]) together with a continuous **generalized force**
$J:I_{0}\to\mathbb R^{n}$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]).
When no force or time interval is prescribed, take $I_0:=\mathbb R$ and
$J(t):=0$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$; in particular this is the convention
for the small-oscillation model in clause (d).
The coordinates $q_{1},\dots,q_{n}$ of $\mathbb R^{n}$ are read in the chart
in which the model is declared and carry declared dimensions
$\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{n}$ and units, and time is read in seconds and mass
in kilograms ([[def-cm01-units]]). The data carry the dimensions

$$[M_{ij}]=\mu\ell^{2}\gamma_{i}^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1},\qquad [K_{ij}]=\mu\ell^{2}\gamma_{i}^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1}\tau^{-2},\qquad [J_{i}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}\gamma_{i}^{-1},$$

so that $\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}Mv$, $\tfrac12q^{\mathsf T}Kq$ and the pairing
$J\cdot\delta q$ of the generalized force with a coordinate variation all have
the energy dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; if the coordinate $q_{i}$ is
length-valued, $\gamma_{i}=\ell$, the entry $J_{i}$ has the force dimension
$\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. This is the dimension bookkeeping of a generalized
coordinate description in the sense of
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]], whose kinetic metric and
generalized forces are the framework objects the data present; the matrices
$M$ and $K$ are model parameters, not measured quantities.

**Fixed-unit numerical convention.** Choose a positive coordinate unit $s_i$ of dimension $\gamma_i$ for each direction, a time unit $t_*>0$ and an energy unit $e_*>0$, held fixed throughout a model calculation. Matrix products, square roots, eigenvectors, derivatives and Euclidean norms below act on numerical coefficients in these units, not on arrays of unlike physical quantities. Explicitly, if $Q_i$, $\mathsf M_{ij}$, $\mathsf K_{ij}$ and $\mathsf J_i$ denote the dimensional data, the symbols in the algebra are
$$q_i=Q_i/s_i,\qquad t=t_{\mathrm{phys}}/t_*,\qquad M_{ij}=\mathsf M_{ij}s_is_j/(e_*t_*^2),\qquad K_{ij}=\mathsf K_{ij}s_is_j/e_*,\qquad J_i=\mathsf J_i s_i/e_*.$$
Then $Mq''+Kq=J$ is exactly the physical equation in these coefficients, $Q_i=s_iq_i$, $\dot Q_i=(s_i/t_*)q_i'$, and the physical energy is $e_*E$. This is an invertible choice of units, imposing no restriction on the dimensions $\gamma_i$. For a variable metric and potential the same convention means $U(q)=U_{\mathrm{phys}}(s_1q_1,\ldots,s_nq_n)/e_*$ and $M_{ij}(q)=\mathsf M_{ij}(s_1q_1,\ldots,s_nq_n)s_is_j/(e_*t_*^2)$. Congruence by the positive diagonal coordinate-scale matrix and multiplication by positive constants preserve symmetry, definiteness and critical-point type.

**(b) Model equation, motions and phase system.** On any interval with
nonempty interior, $C^r$ for $r=1,2$ means that the first $r$ derivatives
exist and are continuous on that interval, using the domain-relative
derivative of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] at included
endpoints; on open intervals this agrees with
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The equation of the model
with data $(M,K,J)$ is

$$M\,q''(t)+K\,q(t)=J(t)\qquad(t\in I_{0}).$$

A **motion** of the model is a curve $q:J\to\mathbb R^{n}$ of class $C^{2}$
on an interval
$J\subseteq I_{0}$ with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) satisfying the
equation for every $t\in J$. A **datum** at $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is a pair
$(q_{0},v_{0})\in\mathbb R^{n}\times\mathbb R^{n}$. The **phase system** of
the model is the first-order linear system $z'=A z+b(t)$ on
$I_{0}\times\mathbb R^{2n}$ with $z=(q,v)$ and

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_{n}\\-M^{-1}K&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad b(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\M^{-1}J(t)\end{pmatrix},$$

where $M^{-1}$ is the inverse of $M$. By the product rule and invertibility of
$M$, a $C^{1}$ curve $t\mapsto(q(t),v(t))$ solves the phase system if and only
if $q$ is a motion of the model and $v=q'$. The model is **free** when
$J\equiv0$ and **forced, with generalized force $J$,** otherwise; the read of
$J$ as a prescribed external generalized force is the modelling status of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] for the external contributions
of a force model.

**(c) Quadratic energies and the mass metric.** The **kinetic energy**, the
**potential energy of the stiffness** and the **mechanical energy** of the
model are

$$T(v):=\tfrac12\,v^{\mathsf T}Mv,\qquad U_{K}(q):=\tfrac12\,q^{\mathsf T}Kq,\qquad E(q,v):=T(v)+U_{K}(q),$$

whose physical readings are $e_*$ times the displayed numerical quantities, all of energy dimension. $U_{K}$ is defined for every symmetric $K$; the name
records that $K$ is the matrix through which the model enters, and when $K$ is
indefinite $U_{K}$ is not non-negative, the model is not presented by a
potential with a local minimum at the origin, and no stability vocabulary is
attached to it by this item. The quadratic form $v\mapsto v^{\mathsf T}Mv$ is
positive definite and is called the **mass metric** of the model; the word
"metric" records only this positive-definiteness, and no distance on
configuration space is defined here.

**(d) Small-oscillation model at an equilibrium.** Let a mechanical system in
a chart be given by a $C^{2}$ field $q\mapsto G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q)$ of
symmetric positive definite matrices on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb
R^{n}$ and a $C^{2}$ potential $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$
([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]), and let
$q_{0}\in\Omega$ be a **mechanical equilibrium**, $\nabla U(q_{0})=0$. Its
**small-oscillation model at $q_{0}$** is the coupled quadratic model with
degrees of freedom $n$, mass metric matrix $M:=G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q_{0})$,
**stiffness matrix** $K_{0}:=D^{2}U(q_{0})$ — the Hessian of the potential
([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], symmetric by
[[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]]) — and zero generalized force, read in the
displacement coordinates $\xi:=q-q_{0}$. When the chart arises from the
generalized-coordinate dictionary of
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]], the matrix
$G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q_{0})=DX(q_{0})^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q_{0})$ is the
value at $q_{0}$ of that dictionary's kinetic metric. This clause assigns
model data to the equilibrium; the identification of the assigned model with
the derivative of the mechanical field, and every statement about its motions,
are separate results and are not asserted here.

**(e) Modal vocabulary of the decoupling data.** All the following matrix operations use the fixed-unit numerical convention. By clauses 1-3 of [[lem-cm-positive-definite-matrix-square-roots]], $M^{1/2}$ and its inverse $M^{-1/2}$ exist and are symmetric positive definite. For every symmetric $K$, without a sign restriction, $S:=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}$ is symmetric, since $S^{\mathsf T}=M^{-1/2}K^{\mathsf T}M^{-1/2}=S$. The [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] therefore supplies an orthogonal $O$ and real diagonal $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$ with $S=O\Lambda O^{\mathsf T}$. This construction includes negative eigenvalues; the restricted non-negative-$K$ result [[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]] is used only in that restricted case. Define **modal coordinates** $z:=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ and **modal vectors** $u_i:=M^{-1/2}Oe_i$, the columns of the inverse transform $q=M^{-1/2}Oz$. The **modal stiffnesses** are the real numbers $\lambda_i$. Direct multiplication gives $Ku_i=\lambda_iMu_i$ and $u_i^{\mathsf T}Mu_j=\delta_{ij}$. In physical units put $a_*:=\sqrt{e_*}\,t_*$. A modal coordinate has unit $a_*$; the $j$-th component of a mass-normalized modal vector has unit $s_j/a_*$, and the physical coordinate is the sum of the physical modal-vector components times their modal amplitudes. The matrix entries of $O$ and its orthonormal eigenvectors are dimensionless numerical coefficients. The physical modal stiffness is $\lambda_i/t_*^2$; an oscillatory or hyperbolic coefficient has unit $a_*$, while the slope coefficient in a zero-mode family $a_i+b_it$ has unit $a_*/t_*$. The physical frequency is $\sqrt{\lambda_i}/t_*$ when $\lambda_i>0$.

An index is **oscillatory** when $\lambda_i>0$, with numerical frequency $\omega_i:=\sqrt{\lambda_i}$; it is a **zero mode** when $\lambda_i=0$, and an **unstable (exponential) direction** when $\lambda_i<0$. Distinct indices are **degenerate** when their stiffnesses agree. For real $\lambda$ define the **modal eigenspace** $E_\lambda:=\ker(K-\lambda M)$. Its dimension is the multiplicity of $\lambda$, because $q\mapsto M^{1/2}q$ bijects it with the $\lambda$-eigenspace of $S$. The model is **oscillatory** when $K$ is non-negative. Indeed $x^{\mathsf T}Sx=(M^{-1/2}x)^{\mathsf T}K(M^{-1/2}x)$, so $K\ge0$ exactly when every $\lambda_i\ge0$; positive definiteness likewise corresponds to all $\lambda_i>0$. The zero-mode multiplicity is $\dim\ker K$. Frequencies are read in radians per unit time under [[def-cm01-units]].

**(f) Status.** This item introduces objects, vocabulary, domains, regularity
and dimensions for the restricted model class of this page and assigns its
small-oscillation model to a mechanical equilibrium. It contains no
existence, uniqueness, conservation, stability, resonance, degeneracy or
approximation assertion; those are proved on this page as separate items. It
adopts no force law of nature and records no measured value. Every later
statement of this page names the data $(M,K,J)$ or the mechanical data
$(G_{\mathrm{kin}},U,q_{0})$ it uses, and the one-dimensional instance is
recorded in the remarks.

Use the fixed coordinate, time and energy units and numerical matrix convention of [[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]]. Every displayed matrix identity and phase norm is in those numerical coordinates; physical positions, velocities, modal amplitudes, frequencies and energies are recovered by the stated fixed scale factors. This does not change the set of physical motions.

For real $u$, define the hyperbolic functions by
$\cosh u:=(e^{u}+e^{-u})/2$ and $\sinh u:=(e^{u}-e^{-u})/2$.

Global-time, growth and boundedness claims below refer to the unique maximal extension of the autonomous free equation on $\mathbb R$; local motions remain its restrictions. Values at $0$ in coefficient formulas are evaluated on that extension when the original interval omits $0$.

Adopt the free coupled quadratic model of
[[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]] with data $(M,K,J)$ in which
$J\equiv0$, $M$ is symmetric positive definite and $K$ is symmetric, with
modal data $M^{1/2}$, $M^{-1/2}$, $O$, $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n})$,
modal coordinates $z=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ and mode frequencies
$\omega_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}$ for $\lambda_{i}>0$. Write
$\kappa_{i}:=\sqrt{-\lambda_{i}}$ for $\lambda_{i}<0$. Then:

1. **Existence and uniqueness on the whole line.** For every $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$
and every datum $(q_{0},v_{0})\in\mathbb R^{2n}$ there is exactly one motion
$q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{n}$ with $q(t_{0})=q_{0}$ and $q'(t_{0})=v_{0}$; it
is the unique maximal motion through that datum.
2. **Complete modal classification.** A curve $q:J\to\mathbb R^{n}$ of class
$C^{2}$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a
motion of the free model if and only if its modal coordinates satisfy

$$z_{i}(t)=a_{i}\cos(\omega_{i}t)+b_{i}\sin(\omega_{i}t)\ (\lambda_{i}>0),\qquad z_{i}(t)=a_{i}+b_{i}t\ (\lambda_{i}=0),\qquad z_{i}(t)=a_{i}\cosh(\kappa_{i}t)+b_{i}\sinh(\kappa_{i}t)\ (\lambda_{i}<0)$$

for real numbers $a_{i},b_{i}$; the coefficients are unique and are
determined by the datum of the unique maximal extension through $a_{i}=z_{i}(0)$, $b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)/\omega_{i}$
for $\lambda_{i}>0$, $b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)$ for $\lambda_{i}=0$ and
$b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)/\kappa_{i}$ for $\lambda_{i}<0$.
3. **Energy and mode energies.** Along every motion the mechanical energy is
constant, and with $E_{i}:=\tfrac12\bigl(z_{i}'^{2}+\lambda_{i}z_{i}^{2}\bigr)$
one has $E(q,q')=\sum_{i=1}^{n}E_{i}$ and every $E_{i}$ is constant; for the
families of clause 2,

$$E_{i}=\tfrac12\omega_{i}^{2}\bigl(a_{i}^{2}+b_{i}^{2}\bigr)\ (\lambda_{i}>0),\qquad E_{i}=\tfrac12b_{i}^{2}\ (\lambda_{i}=0),\qquad E_{i}=\tfrac12\kappa_{i}^{2}\bigl(b_{i}^{2}-a_{i}^{2}\bigr)\ (\lambda_{i}<0).$$

4. **Degenerate families are intrinsic.** Let $\lambda$ be a modal stiffness,
let $E_{\lambda}^{S}:=\{u\in\mathbb R^{n}:M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}u=\lambda u\}$ and
let $N_{\lambda}:=M^{-1/2}E_{\lambda}^{S}$, a subspace of dimension equal to
the multiplicity of $\lambda$. A motion $q$ satisfies $z_{i}\equiv0$ for every
index $i$ with $\lambda_{i}\ne\lambda$ if and only if $q$ is a $C^{2}$ curve
with $q(t)\in N_{\lambda}$ for all $t$ in its interval and $q''+\lambda q=0$.
Consequently the family of such **pure-$\lambda$ motions** is independent of
the choice of diagonalization $O$: for $\lambda>0$ it consists exactly of
$q(t)=\cos(\omega t)q_{0}+\omega^{-1}\sin(\omega t)q_{1}$ with
$q_{0},q_{1}\in N_{\lambda}$ and $\omega=\sqrt{\lambda}$, for $\lambda=0$ of
$q(t)=q_{0}+tq_{1}$ with $q_{0},q_{1}\in N_{\lambda}$, and for $\lambda<0$ of
$q(t)=\cosh(\kappa t)q_{0}+\kappa^{-1}\sinh(\kappa t)q_{1}$ with
$\kappa=\sqrt{-\lambda}$. These formulas on a local interval are restrictions of their unique maximal extensions; $q_0,q_1$ are the position and velocity of that extension at time $0$, even if the local interval omits $0$. The individual modal vectors $u_{i}$ are not
intrinsic when the multiplicity exceeds one.
5. **Boundedness.** If $K$ is positive definite then every motion is bounded
on $\mathbb R$. If $K$ is non-negative and some $\lambda_{i}=0$, then a
motion with $z_{i}'\equiv b_{i}\ne0$ on a zero mode is unbounded on
$[0,\infty)$: the zero mode is affine, not oscillatory.
6. **Unstable direction.** If $K$ is not non-negative, then $(0,0)$ is not a
Lyapunov stable rest point of the free model
([[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]): there is $\varepsilon_{0}>0$
such that for every $\delta>0$ there are data with
$\lVert(q_{0},v_{0})\rVert_{2}<\delta$ whose motion reaches
$\lVert(q(t),q'(t))\rVert_{2}=\varepsilon_{0}$ at some time $t>0$.

The statement is read for the declared model data; no value of any parameter,
no physical realization and no measured frequency is asserted.

The algebra below uses the fixed-unit numerical convention of [[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]], with coordinate units metres, time unit $1\,\mathrm s$ and energy unit $1\,\mathrm J$. Physical model parameters are given their stated units; in matrix products, initial-vector identities and coefficient formulas their numerical coefficients in these fixed units are used. Modal amplitudes have common unit $a_*=(1\,\mathrm J)^{1/2}(1\,\mathrm s)$; the $j$-th component of a mass-normalized modal vector has unit $s_j/a_*$. Modal oscillatory and hyperbolic coefficients have unit $a_*$, and zero-mode slopes have unit $a_*/(1\,\mathrm s)$. Physical coordinates and energies are reconstructed with the coordinate units and $1\,\mathrm J$, respectively. In particular a numerical single-mode datum $q(0)=u_i$ means a modal amplitude of one in this common amplitude unit.

Global-time, growth and boundedness claims below refer to the unique maximal extension of the autonomous free equation on $\mathbb R$; local motions remain its restrictions. Values at $0$ in coefficient formulas are evaluated on that extension when the original interval omits $0$.

Consider two particle labels of equal mass $m>0$ constrained to a line, with
coordinates $x_{1},x_{2}$ in metres read in a fixed inertial frame
([[def-cm01-units]]). Each label is attached to a fixed point by a spring of
stiffness $k>0$ and the labels are coupled to each other by a spring of
stiffness $c>0$; both constants are read in kilograms per second squared.
The model is the coupled quadratic model of
[[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]] with $n=2$, coordinates $q=(x_{1},x_{2})$,
mass metric matrix $M=mI_{2}$ and stiffness

$$K=\begin{pmatrix}k+c&-c\\-c&k+c\end{pmatrix},$$

so that the equation $Mq''+Kq=0$ is the linear chain
$m x_{1}''=-(k+c)x_{1}+cx_{2}$, $m x_{2}''=cx_{1}-(k+c)x_{2}$. Then:

1. the vectors $u_{\pm}:=(1,\pm1)/\sqrt{2m}$ satisfy
$u_{+}^{\mathsf T}Mu_{+}=u_{-}^{\mathsf T}Mu_{-}=1$,
$u_{+}^{\mathsf T}Mu_{-}=0$ and $Ku_{\pm}=\lambda_{\pm}Mu_{\pm}$ with
$$\lambda_{+}=\frac{k}{m},\qquad \lambda_{-}=\frac{k+2c}{m};$$
2. the modal coordinates are $z_{\pm}=e_{\pm}^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ with
$e_{\pm}=(1,\pm1)/\sqrt2$, that is $z_{+}=\sqrt{m/2}\,(x_{1}+x_{2})$ and
$z_{-}=\sqrt{m/2}\,(x_{1}-x_{2})$, and every motion is
$$q(t)=\bigl(A\cos(\omega_{+}t)+B\sin(\omega_{+}t)\bigr)u_{+}+\bigl(C\cos(\omega_{-}t)+D\sin(\omega_{-}t)\bigr)u_{-}$$
with $\omega_{+}=\sqrt{k/m}$ and $\omega_{-}=\sqrt{(k+2c)/m}$;
3. the initial data $q(0)=u_{+}$, $q'(0)=0$ excite exactly the in-phase mode
$q(t)=\cos(\omega_{+}t)u_{+}$, whose mechanical energy is the constant
$E=k/(2m)$; the data $q(0)=u_{-}$, $q'(0)=0$ excite exactly the anti-phase
mode $q(t)=\cos(\omega_{-}t)u_{-}$, with $E=(k+2c)/(2m)$;
4. the in-phase frequency $\omega_{+}$ is independent of the coupling $c$
and the anti-phase frequency $\omega_{-}$ is strictly increasing in $c$;
5. if $k=0$ while $c>0$, then $\lambda_{+}=0$ and $u_{+}$ spans a zero mode:
the general motion is $q(t)=(A+Bt)u_{+}+(C\cos(\omega_{-}t)+D\sin(\omega_{-}t))u_{-}$,
the pair translates freely as a whole and only the relative coordinate
oscillates, at frequency $\sqrt{2c/m}$.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k>0$, and consider the homogeneous damped oscillator model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0$ of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ identically zero, with characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k$, discriminant $\Delta=c^2-4mk$, damping rate $\gamma:=c/(2m)$, and, when applicable, roots
$$\lambda_\pm:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt\Delta}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \lambda:=-\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^2}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0).$$

A local solution here may have any interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. It has a unique extension to the global family below. A **maximal solution** means one that has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval; the maximal solutions of this global autonomous equation are precisely the family members on $\mathbb R$. For a homogeneous model restricted to a time domain $I$, its solutions have $J\subseteq I$ and are restrictions of these same global members; their extensions solve the all-$\mathbb R$ equation.

1. **Distinct real roots.** If $\Delta>0$, then $\lambda_+>\lambda_-$ are exactly the real roots of $p$, and a function $x:J\to\mathbb R$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a solution of the model if and only if
$$x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_+t}+Be^{\lambda_-t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

2. **Double real root.** If $\Delta=0$, then $\lambda=-c/(2m)$ is the only root of $p$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{\lambda t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

3. **Complex conjugate roots.** If $\Delta<0$, then $\omega>0$, the roots of $p$ are $-\gamma\pm i\omega$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)\bigr)\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

4. **Initial data.** In each of the three cases and for every $(x_0,v_0)\in\mathbb R^2$ there is exactly one solution $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$ and $x'(0)=v_0$. Its coefficients are
$$A=\frac{v_0-\lambda_-x_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-},\quad B=\frac{\lambda_+x_0-v_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}\quad(\Delta>0),\qquad A=x_0,\ B=v_0-\lambda x_0\quad(\Delta=0),$$
$$A=x_0,\quad B=\frac{v_0+\gamma x_0}{\omega}\quad(\Delta<0).$$

derivations.claim: Degeneracy: by [F4] the matrix $M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}$ is $(k/m)I_{2}$, whose only eigenvalue is $k/m$ with eigenspace $\mathbb R^{2}$; any orthonormal basis diagonalizes it because a scalar matrix commutes with every matrix. Hence $\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=k/m$, $E_{\lambda}=\mathbb R^{2}$, $N_{\lambda}=\mathbb R^{2}$ and the decoupling data of clause (e) of [[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]] are non-unique. This is clause 1.

Motions: by [F2] and [F5] the motions are the superpositions of the scalar families with the single frequency $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$ in every direction, i.e. the displayed four-parameter family $q(t)=\cos(\omega t)a+\sin(\omega t)b$; the datum $q(0)=a$, $q'(0)=0$ corresponds to $b=0$ and gives $q(t)=\cos(\omega t)a$, a motion whose values lie in the line spanned by $a$ for all $t$: by clause 4 of [F2] this is a pure-$\lambda$ motion, and every nonzero $a$ gives one. This is clause 2.

Splitting by coupling: the stiffness of [F3] reduces to $kI_{2}$ at $c=0$, so the data of this example and of the coupled two-mass model agree at $c=0$; for $c>0$, [F3] gives the distinct modal stiffnesses $k/m$ (the in-phase mode, unchanged by the coupling) and $(k+2c)/m$ (the relative motion, raised by the coupling). This is clause 4.

Intrinsic versus non-intrinsic data: the number $\lambda=k/m$ and the subspace $N_{\lambda}=\mathbb R^{2}$ are determined by $M$ and $K$ alone, whereas an individual modal vector is a member of a chosen orthonormal basis and different admissible decouplings assign the same motion different coordinate labels; hence no basis-independent decomposition of the four-parameter family into two distinguished one-parameter families exists here. This is clause 3.

Clauses 1-4 are verified on the explicit data; the splitting statement is a comparison of two explicitly specified models at different parameter values and is not a general assertion that degeneracies are always removed by perturbations.

boundaries.reason: The oscillator subspace is the prescribed finite-dimensional repeated-frequency eigenspace, whose displayed independent vectors make it nonempty.

boundaries.evidence: The zero displacement and zero velocity data are included in the four-parameter family of step 2.1; the stiffness itself is positive definite.

boundaries.reason: The example is a two-degree-of-freedom instance; its whole point is the repeated eigenvalue, so no scalar case is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: The double eigenvalue λ=k/m with two-dimensional eigenspace is the subject of clauses 1-3 and steps 1.1-3.1.

boundaries.reason: No interval endpoints occur: motions are asserted on R and the comparison of step 2.2 concerns two parameter values.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $M:\Omega\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $M(q)$ symmetric and positive definite for every $q\in\Omega$, that is $v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$. The matrix field $M$ is the **kinetic metric field** and $U$ the **potential** of the data in the chart $\Omega$.

Define, for $(q,v)\in\Omega\times\mathbb R^n$, the **kinetic energy**, **Lagrangian** and **energy**

$$T(q,v):=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v,\qquad L(q,v):=T(q,v)-U(q),\qquad E(q,v):=T(q,v)+U(q),$$

and, for $q\in\Omega$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the matrix

$$D_qM(q)[v]:=\sum_{k=1}^nv_k\,\partial_kM(q),\qquad\bigl(\partial_kM(q)\bigr)_{ij}=\partial_kM_{ij}(q).$$

The **mechanical vector field** of the data is the map

$$G:\Omega\times\mathbb R^n\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n,\qquad G(q,v)=\Bigl(v,\ M(q)^{-1}\bigl(\tfrac12\nabla_q(v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v)-\bigl(D_qM(q)[v]\bigr)v-\nabla U(q)\bigr)\Bigr),$$

where $\nabla_q$ and $\nabla U$ are Euclidean gradients ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and $M(q)^{-1}$ is the inverse of the positive definite matrix $M(q)$ ([[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]], [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). The **mechanical system** in the chart is the first-order system

$$q'(t)=v(t),\qquad v'(t)=M(q(t))^{-1}\Bigl(\tfrac12\nabla_qf\bigl(q(t),v(t)\bigr)-\bigl(D_qM(q(t))[v(t)]\bigr)v(t)-\nabla U(q(t))\Bigr),\qquad f(q,v):=v^{\mathsf T}M(q)v .$$

A point $q_* \in\Omega$ is a **mechanical equilibrium** when $\nabla U(q_*)=0$.

**(a) Data of a coupled quadratic model.** A **coupled quadratic model** (a
**quadratic oscillator model**) is declared by the following data: an integer
$n\ge1$, the number of **degrees of freedom**; a **mass metric matrix**
$M\in M_{n}(\mathbb R)$, symmetric and positive definite, that is
$M=M^{\mathsf T}$ and $v^{\mathsf T}Mv>0$ for every nonzero
$v\in\mathbb R^{n}$ ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); a **stiffness matrix**
$K\in M_{n}(\mathbb R)$, symmetric, $K=K^{\mathsf T}$; and an interval $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior
([[def-interval]]) together with a continuous **generalized force**
$J:I_{0}\to\mathbb R^{n}$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]).
When no force or time interval is prescribed, take $I_0:=\mathbb R$ and
$J(t):=0$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$; in particular this is the convention
for the small-oscillation model in clause (d).
The coordinates $q_{1},\dots,q_{n}$ of $\mathbb R^{n}$ are read in the chart
in which the model is declared and carry declared dimensions
$\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{n}$ and units, and time is read in seconds and mass
in kilograms ([[def-cm01-units]]). The data carry the dimensions

$$[M_{ij}]=\mu\ell^{2}\gamma_{i}^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1},\qquad [K_{ij}]=\mu\ell^{2}\gamma_{i}^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1}\tau^{-2},\qquad [J_{i}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}\gamma_{i}^{-1},$$

so that $\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}Mv$, $\tfrac12q^{\mathsf T}Kq$ and the pairing
$J\cdot\delta q$ of the generalized force with a coordinate variation all have
the energy dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; if the coordinate $q_{i}$ is
length-valued, $\gamma_{i}=\ell$, the entry $J_{i}$ has the force dimension
$\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. This is the dimension bookkeeping of a generalized
coordinate description in the sense of
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]], whose kinetic metric and
generalized forces are the framework objects the data present; the matrices
$M$ and $K$ are model parameters, not measured quantities.

**Fixed-unit numerical convention.** Choose a positive coordinate unit $s_i$ of dimension $\gamma_i$ for each direction, a time unit $t_*>0$ and an energy unit $e_*>0$, held fixed throughout a model calculation. Matrix products, square roots, eigenvectors, derivatives and Euclidean norms below act on numerical coefficients in these units, not on arrays of unlike physical quantities. Explicitly, if $Q_i$, $\mathsf M_{ij}$, $\mathsf K_{ij}$ and $\mathsf J_i$ denote the dimensional data, the symbols in the algebra are
$$q_i=Q_i/s_i,\qquad t=t_{\mathrm{phys}}/t_*,\qquad M_{ij}=\mathsf M_{ij}s_is_j/(e_*t_*^2),\qquad K_{ij}=\mathsf K_{ij}s_is_j/e_*,\qquad J_i=\mathsf J_i s_i/e_*.$$
Then $Mq''+Kq=J$ is exactly the physical equation in these coefficients, $Q_i=s_iq_i$, $\dot Q_i=(s_i/t_*)q_i'$, and the physical energy is $e_*E$. This is an invertible choice of units, imposing no restriction on the dimensions $\gamma_i$. For a variable metric and potential the same convention means $U(q)=U_{\mathrm{phys}}(s_1q_1,\ldots,s_nq_n)/e_*$ and $M_{ij}(q)=\mathsf M_{ij}(s_1q_1,\ldots,s_nq_n)s_is_j/(e_*t_*^2)$. Congruence by the positive diagonal coordinate-scale matrix and multiplication by positive constants preserve symmetry, definiteness and critical-point type.

**(b) Model equation, motions and phase system.** On any interval with
nonempty interior, $C^r$ for $r=1,2$ means that the first $r$ derivatives
exist and are continuous on that interval, using the domain-relative
derivative of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] at included
endpoints; on open intervals this agrees with
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. The equation of the model
with data $(M,K,J)$ is

$$M\,q''(t)+K\,q(t)=J(t)\qquad(t\in I_{0}).$$

A **motion** of the model is a curve $q:J\to\mathbb R^{n}$ of class $C^{2}$
on an interval
$J\subseteq I_{0}$ with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) satisfying the
equation for every $t\in J$. A **datum** at $t_{0}\in I_{0}$ is a pair
$(q_{0},v_{0})\in\mathbb R^{n}\times\mathbb R^{n}$. The **phase system** of
the model is the first-order linear system $z'=A z+b(t)$ on
$I_{0}\times\mathbb R^{2n}$ with $z=(q,v)$ and

$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_{n}\\-M^{-1}K&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad b(t)=\begin{pmatrix}0\\M^{-1}J(t)\end{pmatrix},$$

where $M^{-1}$ is the inverse of $M$. By the product rule and invertibility of
$M$, a $C^{1}$ curve $t\mapsto(q(t),v(t))$ solves the phase system if and only
if $q$ is a motion of the model and $v=q'$. The model is **free** when
$J\equiv0$ and **forced, with generalized force $J$,** otherwise; the read of
$J$ as a prescribed external generalized force is the modelling status of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] for the external contributions
of a force model.

**(c) Quadratic energies and the mass metric.** The **kinetic energy**, the
**potential energy of the stiffness** and the **mechanical energy** of the
model are

$$T(v):=\tfrac12\,v^{\mathsf T}Mv,\qquad U_{K}(q):=\tfrac12\,q^{\mathsf T}Kq,\qquad E(q,v):=T(v)+U_{K}(q),$$

whose physical readings are $e_*$ times the displayed numerical quantities, all of energy dimension. $U_{K}$ is defined for every symmetric $K$; the name
records that $K$ is the matrix through which the model enters, and when $K$ is
indefinite $U_{K}$ is not non-negative, the model is not presented by a
potential with a local minimum at the origin, and no stability vocabulary is
attached to it by this item. The quadratic form $v\mapsto v^{\mathsf T}Mv$ is
positive definite and is called the **mass metric** of the model; the word
"metric" records only this positive-definiteness, and no distance on
configuration space is defined here.

**(d) Small-oscillation model at an equilibrium.** Let a mechanical system in
a chart be given by a $C^{2}$ field $q\mapsto G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q)$ of
symmetric positive definite matrices on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb
R^{n}$ and a $C^{2}$ potential $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R$
([[def-cm-mechanical-vector-field-and-energy-in-a-chart]]), and let
$q_{0}\in\Omega$ be a **mechanical equilibrium**, $\nabla U(q_{0})=0$. Its
**small-oscillation model at $q_{0}$** is the coupled quadratic model with
degrees of freedom $n$, mass metric matrix $M:=G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q_{0})$,
**stiffness matrix** $K_{0}:=D^{2}U(q_{0})$ — the Hessian of the potential
([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], symmetric by
[[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]]) — and zero generalized force, read in the
displacement coordinates $\xi:=q-q_{0}$. When the chart arises from the
generalized-coordinate dictionary of
[[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]], the matrix
$G_{\mathrm{kin}}(q_{0})=DX(q_{0})^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q_{0})$ is the
value at $q_{0}$ of that dictionary's kinetic metric. This clause assigns
model data to the equilibrium; the identification of the assigned model with
the derivative of the mechanical field, and every statement about its motions,
are separate results and are not asserted here.

**(e) Modal vocabulary of the decoupling data.** All the following matrix operations use the fixed-unit numerical convention. By clauses 1-3 of [[lem-cm-positive-definite-matrix-square-roots]], $M^{1/2}$ and its inverse $M^{-1/2}$ exist and are symmetric positive definite. For every symmetric $K$, without a sign restriction, $S:=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}$ is symmetric, since $S^{\mathsf T}=M^{-1/2}K^{\mathsf T}M^{-1/2}=S$. The [[cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms]] therefore supplies an orthogonal $O$ and real diagonal $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$ with $S=O\Lambda O^{\mathsf T}$. This construction includes negative eigenvalues; the restricted non-negative-$K$ result [[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]] is used only in that restricted case. Define **modal coordinates** $z:=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ and **modal vectors** $u_i:=M^{-1/2}Oe_i$, the columns of the inverse transform $q=M^{-1/2}Oz$. The **modal stiffnesses** are the real numbers $\lambda_i$. Direct multiplication gives $Ku_i=\lambda_iMu_i$ and $u_i^{\mathsf T}Mu_j=\delta_{ij}$. In physical units put $a_*:=\sqrt{e_*}\,t_*$. A modal coordinate has unit $a_*$; the $j$-th component of a mass-normalized modal vector has unit $s_j/a_*$, and the physical coordinate is the sum of the physical modal-vector components times their modal amplitudes. The matrix entries of $O$ and its orthonormal eigenvectors are dimensionless numerical coefficients. The physical modal stiffness is $\lambda_i/t_*^2$; an oscillatory or hyperbolic coefficient has unit $a_*$, while the slope coefficient in a zero-mode family $a_i+b_it$ has unit $a_*/t_*$. The physical frequency is $\sqrt{\lambda_i}/t_*$ when $\lambda_i>0$.

An index is **oscillatory** when $\lambda_i>0$, with numerical frequency $\omega_i:=\sqrt{\lambda_i}$; it is a **zero mode** when $\lambda_i=0$, and an **unstable (exponential) direction** when $\lambda_i<0$. Distinct indices are **degenerate** when their stiffnesses agree. For real $\lambda$ define the **modal eigenspace** $E_\lambda:=\ker(K-\lambda M)$. Its dimension is the multiplicity of $\lambda$, because $q\mapsto M^{1/2}q$ bijects it with the $\lambda$-eigenspace of $S$. The model is **oscillatory** when $K$ is non-negative. Indeed $x^{\mathsf T}Sx=(M^{-1/2}x)^{\mathsf T}K(M^{-1/2}x)$, so $K\ge0$ exactly when every $\lambda_i\ge0$; positive definiteness likewise corresponds to all $\lambda_i>0$. The zero-mode multiplicity is $\dim\ker K$. Frequencies are read in radians per unit time under [[def-cm01-units]].

**(f) Status.** This item introduces objects, vocabulary, domains, regularity
and dimensions for the restricted model class of this page and assigns its
small-oscillation model to a mechanical equilibrium. It contains no
existence, uniqueness, conservation, stability, resonance, degeneracy or
approximation assertion; those are proved on this page as separate items. It
adopts no force law of nature and records no measured value. Every later
statement of this page names the data $(M,K,J)$ or the mechanical data
$(G_{\mathrm{kin}},U,q_{0})$ it uses, and the one-dimensional instance is
recorded in the remarks.

Use the fixed coordinate, time and energy units and numerical matrix convention of [[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]]. Every displayed matrix identity and phase norm is in those numerical coordinates; physical positions, velocities, modal amplitudes, frequencies and energies are recovered by the stated fixed scale factors. This does not change the set of physical motions.

For real $u$, define the hyperbolic functions by
$\cosh u:=(e^{u}+e^{-u})/2$ and $\sinh u:=(e^{u}-e^{-u})/2$.

Global-time, growth and boundedness claims below refer to the unique maximal extension of the autonomous free equation on $\mathbb R$; local motions remain its restrictions. Values at $0$ in coefficient formulas are evaluated on that extension when the original interval omits $0$.

Adopt the free coupled quadratic model of
[[def-cm09-coupled-quadratic-model]] with data $(M,K,J)$ in which
$J\equiv0$, $M$ is symmetric positive definite and $K$ is symmetric, with
modal data $M^{1/2}$, $M^{-1/2}$, $O$, $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{n})$,
modal coordinates $z=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$ and mode frequencies
$\omega_{i}=\sqrt{\lambda_{i}}$ for $\lambda_{i}>0$. Write
$\kappa_{i}:=\sqrt{-\lambda_{i}}$ for $\lambda_{i}<0$. Then:

1. **Existence and uniqueness on the whole line.** For every $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$
and every datum $(q_{0},v_{0})\in\mathbb R^{2n}$ there is exactly one motion
$q:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{n}$ with $q(t_{0})=q_{0}$ and $q'(t_{0})=v_{0}$; it
is the unique maximal motion through that datum.
2. **Complete modal classification.** A curve $q:J\to\mathbb R^{n}$ of class
$C^{2}$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a
motion of the free model if and only if its modal coordinates satisfy

$$z_{i}(t)=a_{i}\cos(\omega_{i}t)+b_{i}\sin(\omega_{i}t)\ (\lambda_{i}>0),\qquad z_{i}(t)=a_{i}+b_{i}t\ (\lambda_{i}=0),\qquad z_{i}(t)=a_{i}\cosh(\kappa_{i}t)+b_{i}\sinh(\kappa_{i}t)\ (\lambda_{i}<0)$$

for real numbers $a_{i},b_{i}$; the coefficients are unique and are
determined by the datum of the unique maximal extension through $a_{i}=z_{i}(0)$, $b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)/\omega_{i}$
for $\lambda_{i}>0$, $b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)$ for $\lambda_{i}=0$ and
$b_{i}=z_{i}'(0)/\kappa_{i}$ for $\lambda_{i}<0$.
3. **Energy and mode energies.** Along every motion the mechanical energy is
constant, and with $E_{i}:=\tfrac12\bigl(z_{i}'^{2}+\lambda_{i}z_{i}^{2}\bigr)$
one has $E(q,q')=\sum_{i=1}^{n}E_{i}$ and every $E_{i}$ is constant; for the
families of clause 2,

$$E_{i}=\tfrac12\omega_{i}^{2}\bigl(a_{i}^{2}+b_{i}^{2}\bigr)\ (\lambda_{i}>0),\qquad E_{i}=\tfrac12b_{i}^{2}\ (\lambda_{i}=0),\qquad E_{i}=\tfrac12\kappa_{i}^{2}\bigl(b_{i}^{2}-a_{i}^{2}\bigr)\ (\lambda_{i}<0).$$

4. **Degenerate families are intrinsic.** Let $\lambda$ be a modal stiffness,
let $E_{\lambda}^{S}:=\{u\in\mathbb R^{n}:M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}u=\lambda u\}$ and
let $N_{\lambda}:=M^{-1/2}E_{\lambda}^{S}$, a subspace of dimension equal to
the multiplicity of $\lambda$. A motion $q$ satisfies $z_{i}\equiv0$ for every
index $i$ with $\lambda_{i}\ne\lambda$ if and only if $q$ is a $C^{2}$ curve
with $q(t)\in N_{\lambda}$ for all $t$ in its interval and $q''+\lambda q=0$.
Consequently the family of such **pure-$\lambda$ motions** is independent of
the choice of diagonalization $O$: for $\lambda>0$ it consists exactly of
$q(t)=\cos(\omega t)q_{0}+\omega^{-1}\sin(\omega t)q_{1}$ with
$q_{0},q_{1}\in N_{\lambda}$ and $\omega=\sqrt{\lambda}$, for $\lambda=0$ of
$q(t)=q_{0}+tq_{1}$ with $q_{0},q_{1}\in N_{\lambda}$, and for $\lambda<0$ of
$q(t)=\cosh(\kappa t)q_{0}+\kappa^{-1}\sinh(\kappa t)q_{1}$ with
$\kappa=\sqrt{-\lambda}$. These formulas on a local interval are restrictions of their unique maximal extensions; $q_0,q_1$ are the position and velocity of that extension at time $0$, even if the local interval omits $0$. The individual modal vectors $u_{i}$ are not
intrinsic when the multiplicity exceeds one.
5. **Boundedness.** If $K$ is positive definite then every motion is bounded
on $\mathbb R$. If $K$ is non-negative and some $\lambda_{i}=0$, then a
motion with $z_{i}'\equiv b_{i}\ne0$ on a zero mode is unbounded on
$[0,\infty)$: the zero mode is affine, not oscillatory.
6. **Unstable direction.** If $K$ is not non-negative, then $(0,0)$ is not a
Lyapunov stable rest point of the free model
([[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]): there is $\varepsilon_{0}>0$
such that for every $\delta>0$ there are data with
$\lVert(q_{0},v_{0})\rVert_{2}<\delta$ whose motion reaches
$\lVert(q(t),q'(t))\rVert_{2}=\varepsilon_{0}$ at some time $t>0$.

The statement is read for the declared model data; no value of any parameter,
no physical realization and no measured frequency is asserted.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $0\in U$, and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $F(0)=0$. Put $A:=DF(0)$ ([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) and suppose that

- no complex eigenvalue of $A$ ([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]) has real part $0$, and
- at least one eigenvalue of $A$ has positive real part.

Then the equilibrium $0$ is not Lyapunov stable ([[def-cm-equilibrium-and-lyapunov-stability]]): there is a real number $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that for every $\delta>0$ there exist $z_0\in U$ with $\|z_0\|_2<\delta$ and a time $t_1>0$ such that the maximal solution $z$ of $z'=F(z)$, $z(0)=z_0$ is defined on $[0,t_1]$ and satisfies

$$\|z(t_1)\|_2=\varepsilon_0 .$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be a map. Consider the autonomous first-order system

$$z'(t)=F(z(t)),$$

read as the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] with $D=\mathbb R\times U$ and right-hand side $(t,z)\mapsto F(z)$. A **solution** below means a solution of this system on an interval containing $0$; a solution whose interval is $[0,\infty)$ or contains it is said to be **defined for all $t\ge0$**.

A solution $\tilde z:J\to U$ **extends** $z:I\to U$ when $I\subseteq J$ and $\tilde z|_I=z$; the extension is proper if $I\subsetneq J$. A solution is **maximal** when it has no proper extension ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]]). All stability predicates below quantify over maximal solutions whose intervals contain $0$; their local restrictions remain solutions. This convention asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of maximal solutions for an arbitrary map $F$.

A point $z_*\in U$ is an **equilibrium** (also **fixed point** or **zero**) of $F$ when $F(z_*)=0$; then the constant function $z(t)=z_*$ is a solution on every interval containing $0$.

Let $z_*\in U$ be an equilibrium.

1. $z_*$ is **Lyapunov stable** (or simply **stable**) when for every Euclidean ball $B_\varepsilon(z_*)$ with $\overline{B_\varepsilon(z_*)}\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) there is $\delta\in(0,\varepsilon]$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\|z(0)-z_*\|_2<\delta$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies

$$\|z(t)-z_*\|_2<\varepsilon\qquad(t\ge0).$$

2. $z_*$ is **asymptotically stable** when it is Lyapunov stable and in addition there is $\delta_0>0$ such that every maximal solution $z$ with $\|z(0)-z_*\|_2<\delta_0$ is defined for all $t\ge0$ and satisfies $\|z(t)-z_*\|_2\to0$ as $t\to\infty$.

An equilibrium which is not Lyapunov stable is **unstable**. An equilibrium is **globally asymptotically stable** when it is asymptotically stable and every maximal solution of the system is defined for all $t\ge0$ and converges to it as $t\to\infty$.

Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, let $k\le0$, and consider the model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0$ of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ identically zero. In the three cases below, $x:J\to\mathbb R$ runs over solutions on intervals $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior.

A local solution here may have any interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. It has a unique extension to the global family below. A **maximal solution** means one that has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval; the maximal solutions of this global autonomous equation are precisely the family members on $\mathbb R$. For a homogeneous model restricted to a time domain $I$, its solutions have $J\subseteq I$ and are restrictions of these same global members; their extensions solve the all-$\mathbb R$ equation.

1. **Double zero root ($k=0$, $c=0$).** Then on every such interval $J$, $x$ solves the model if and only if $x(t)=A+Bt$ for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$; each such local solution is the restriction of a unique global member of this family. For every datum $(x_0,v_0)$ there is a unique global solution on $\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$, $x'(0)=v_0$, namely $x(t)=x_0+v_0t$.
2. **Simple zero root ($k=0$, $c>0$).** Then on every such interval $J$, $x$ solves the model if and only if
$$x(t)=A+Be^{-ct/m}$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$; each such local solution is the restriction of a unique global member of this family. For every datum $(x_0,v_0)$ there is a unique global solution on $\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$, $x'(0)=v_0$, namely the member with $A=x_0+\frac{m v_0}{c}$ and $B=-\frac{m v_0}{c}$. This global solution has limit $A$ as $t\to+\infty$; any local solution on an interval unbounded above has the same limit along that interval.
3. **One positive and one negative root ($k<0$).** Put $$\lambda_\pm:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt{c^2-4mk}}{2m}.$$ Then $\lambda_-<0<\lambda_+$, both are real roots of the characteristic polynomial, and on every such interval $J$, $x$ solves the model if and only if
$$x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_+t}+Be^{\lambda_-t}$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$; each such local solution is the restriction of a global member of this family. In particular the global solution $t\mapsto e^{\lambda_+t}$ has data $x(0)=1$, $x'(0)=\lambda_+$ and satisfies $e^{\lambda_+t}\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$: the model has an unbounded solution growing exponentially on $[0,\infty)$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

derivations.claim: Equilibrium and stiffness: $U'(\theta)=-mgl\sin\theta$ vanishes at $\theta=0$, and $U(\theta)<U(0)$ for $0<\lvert\theta\rvert<\pi$ on the chart, so $\theta=0$ is a strict local maximum and $K=U''(0)=-mgl<0$; the small-oscillation model has data $M=ml^{2}$, $K=-mgl$, i.e. modal stiffness $\lambda=-g/l$. This is clause 1.

Exponential families: by [F3] and [F5] the motions of the quadratic model are exactly $\xi(t)=a\cosh(\kappa t)+d\sinh(\kappa t)$ with $\kappa=\sqrt{g/l}$; for the datum $\xi(0)=0$, $\xi'(0)=b\ne0$ the hyperbolic coefficients are $a=0$ and $d=b/\kappa$, so the motion is $(b/\kappa)\sinh(\kappa t)$, which is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$. This is clause 2.

Nonlinear instability: the field $F(\theta,v)=(v,(g/l)\sin\theta)$ is $C^{1}$ on $\mathbb R^{2}$ with $F(0,0)=0$; by [F6] its derivative at the origin has the real eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt{g/l}$, none on the imaginary axis and one positive, so the hypotheses of [F4] hold and $(0,0)$ is not a Lyapunov stable equilibrium of the pendulum chart system. This is clause 4.

Quadratic instability: by clause 6 of [F3] applied to the one-dimensional free model with negative modal stiffness, the rest point is not Lyapunov stable, with the displayed escaping family; explicitly, for every $\delta>0$ choose $0<\lvert b\rvert<\min(\delta,1)$. The motion $(b/\kappa)\sinh(\kappa t)$ has initial phase norm $|b|<1$ and its position norm is unbounded by [F5]. Thus its continuous phase norm starts below $1$ and exceeds $1$ at some finite time; [F7] gives a time $t>0$ at which the phase norm is exactly $1=\varepsilon_0$. This is clause 3.

Clauses 1-4 are verified on the explicit chart data; clause 4 is the nonlinear conclusion supplied by the hyperbolic-saddle theorem, whereas clause 3 concerns the quadratic model alone. The parameters $m,l,g$ are model data, and no escape time, measured period or apparatus behaviour is asserted.

boundaries.reason: The unstable quadratic Example specifies a negative stiffness direction and a positive mass, so the exponential mode is an inhabited scalar solution family.

boundaries.evidence: The zero displacement datum and zero velocity are included; the escaping family of step 3.1 starts from (0,b) with b small.
The example is exactly the scalar one-degree-of-freedom case; clause 6 of the free-mode theorem is instantiated at λ=-g/l in step 3.1.

boundaries.reason: The single modal stiffness -g/l is nonzero and simple, so no degeneracy arises.

boundaries.evidence: The escaping motion is evaluated on the forward halfline [0,infinity) in steps 2.1 and 3.1; no endpoint derivative is asserted.

boundaries.reason: The hyperbolic-sine growing curve is explicitly given by its small initial velocity; the instability witness does not require simultaneous choices of perturbed motions.
This Example exhibits growth in a negative-stiffness mode; it does not assert that every unstable nonlinear model must have this quadratic mechanism.
